reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
In this study, Jia et al. provide an extensive assessment of the role of the anterior piriform cortex in mediating the analgesic effect of innate fear. The topic is highly interesting but complex as it is not easy to conceptually link the impact of innate fear on pain sensation. To do so the authors exposed mice to the odor of predators and then proceed to a battery of pain-related tests, showing that animals previously exposed to the odor predator exhibit reduced nocifensive behavioral responses.
Using an extensive combination of anatomical, imaging, and functional approaches they progressively identify a GABAergic projections from the anterior proportion of the piriform cortex to the mediodorsal thalamus that may be both necessary and sufficient for this effect. This result calls for partcular attention since long-distance inhibitory projections from cortex to the MD has never been reported before in mice. The amount of experimental work is impressive and all approaches are by themselves state-of-the-art, but the meaning and interpretation of all these experiments also appear as somewhat questionable. In addition, crucial methodological details are missing as explained below.
Methodology/behavioral paradigm
The exact protocol for odor exposure is not clear enough in relation with the many experiments reported. When exactly and for how long are animals exposed to the different odours? Is it acute or multiple exposures? Is it during each beahvioral assay or just before? Dpending on the answers to these questions there may be new issues to consider. Too many crucial details are lacking preventing the reader from understanding what exactly has been done.
For all histological controls, not enough data are provided to document the spread of viral infusion. For all interventions (DREADD and opto), general histology should be provided showing shades of spread for each included individual as is usually the norm.
Without these essential controls/information, the conceptual ground of the whole paper is unclear.
GABAergic projection from cortex to thalamus
The authors should really comment on whether this was expected or not. Very importantly, greater care is needed to ensure that this important claim is unambiguously supported by included data.
For example, neurons that are positive for vgat may also transmit glutamate, how do we know if that is not the case here?
Viral spread into TRN which is mentionned in the paper is guaranteed to yield thalamic inhibition but this is not taken into consideration. The authors also reasonned that there is a higher proportion of GAD2+ proportion of cells labelled for dtomato than it is for CamKII cells (Figure 2c and 2d, the first d should be c though) but the panel c shows very few GAD2+ cells whereas CAMKII+ cells are abundant. This casts further doubt on that inhibitory CT route which would be further fraction at best of those GAD2+ cells (those projecting to the MD). All these issues add on each other, making the whole point not compelling given the importance of the claim.
Taken together, these issues largely undermine the paper to the extent that it is unclear whether the main points could still hold if they can be adequately addressed and making any more minor comments irrelevant at this stage. The paper would also benefit from professional level proof-reading for english.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
The manuscript by Jia et al. describes a very interesting set of findings revealing a potential circuit underlying pain suppression by innate fear. Of particular interest this is a novel long-range GABAergic projection originating from Anterior Piriform Cortex (APC) and targeting MD thalamus. While I think the basic story is sound, there are some issues with statistical comparisons and the interpretation of results that need to be addressed. In addition, it is unclear how the slice results relate to the behavioral results – there are questions about how exactly manipulations were done and what were the possible mechanisms that lead to long-lasting effects of 2MT exposure / chemogenetic inhibition persisting into slice experiments.
1. It would be useful to know what % of APC neurons activated by fear are a) GABAergic, b) project to MD, and c) are both.
2. For 4e – what was the protocol for 2MT exposure? Specifically what was the frequency and duration of 2MT exposure, and what was the timing relative to brain slice preparation? What do the authors think is the mechanism underlying this effect?
3. The causal demonstration of the role of this circuit is in Fig. 5 and 6. Fig. 5 shows that chemogenetically inhibiting MD-projecting GABAergic neurons in APC increases pain sensitivity in normal mice and SNI mice exposed to 2MT. Fig. 5g-i show that chemogenetic inhibition of GABAergic APC-MD neurons increases the excitability of MD neurons in 2MT-exposed SNI mice.
a. The protocol for 2MT exposure and chemogenetic inhibition are not explained. Specifically what was the frequency and duration of 2MT exposure? What was the timing of 2MT exposure relative to brain slice preparation? Was chemogenetic inhibition done preceding/during every 2MT exposure, and if not, what was the timing of chemogenetic inhibition relative to 2MT exposure?
b. Does the effect of chemogenetic inhibition on MD neuron excitability depend on 2MT exposure, or does the same effect occur in mice which undergo chemogenetic inhibition but have not been exposed to 2MT? This seems like an important and straightforward experiment.
c. What is the possible mechanism for this? Was there a change in input resistance suggestive of increases in spontaneous inhibitory input (potentially from GABAergic APC-MD terminals) in MD neurons? Did the authors measure spontaneous inhibitory input? This mechanism is important because it’s hard to imagine how transient inhibition of an inhibitory input would end up leading to persistent changes in the excitability of MD neurons.
4. Fig. 6 shows that inhibition of GABAergic APC-MD terminals increases pain sensitivity in mice exposed to 2MT +/- SNI. Based on Supp. Fig 6+7, it seems that the effect is really the same regardless of whether mice have been exposed to 2MT and/or SNI – inhibiting these cells always leads to an exacerbation of pain sensitivity (albeit this effect is smaller in absence of 2MT). So it’s not just that it abolishes the effects of 2MT, but it also seems to increase pain sensitivity at baseline – this is an important point that should be noted explicitly and clearly.
5. Based on Supp Fig. 6c, inhibiting APC-MD GABAergic neurons increases CPA. This means that inhibiting these neurons is aversive, independent of pain. Conversely increases in the activity of these neurons are probably rewarding. This is a caveat that makes the interpretation of Fig. 6i less clear – specifically, the CPP shown in Fig. 6i may not be related to an alleviation of pain but rather to independent rewarding effects of the stimulation.
6. It’s a bit odd to use 20Hz pulse trains to activate eNpHR – its kinetics are too slow to respond to these pulse trains so it’s a bit better / simpler to just use continuous light. Related to this, was the reported light power the peak light power, i.e., each pulse reaches a peak of 5 mW, or was the reported light power of 5 mW the net / average power measured over light ON and light OFF periods?
7. Line 209 – the authors should not report “a trend towards a statistically significant decrease.” The decrease is not statistically significant. They can say that this was a trend that did not reach statistical significance, or they can perform additional experiments to increase the n to confirm that the result does / does not reach statistical significance.
8. Related to this, almost all of the statistical tests are performed as comparisons within a group on two days, where the author report significant changes in the experimental group but not in the control group. Really, this is not appropriate – the authors should perform statistical tests which directly compare the experimental and control groups, either using a 2-way ANOVA, or by calculating a difference score for each animal across the two days and then comparing these difference scores between the experimental and control groups to show a significant difference. I think the authors need to do this, if not in all cases, for their key findings.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
In this manuscript by Jia and colleagues, the authors investigate the neural mechanisms by which innate fear suppresses pain sensitivity in male mice, identifying a GABAergic projection from the anterior piriform cortex (APC) to the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) as a key component. Using a combination of viral tracing, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, chemogenetics, and optogenetics, the authors claim to show that innate fear—triggered by predator odor (2MT)—induces analgesia via this corticothalamic circuit.
While the study is methodologically rich and addresses an important topic, several conceptual, methodological, and interpretive issues significantly dampened the excitement about the manuscript and its current impact. The manuscript overstates its mechanistic conclusions. In my opinion, the core effects observed are better interpreted as modulations of pain sensitivity, rather than evidence of a distinct analgesic state induced by innate fear.
Major points:
1. The manuscript relies on the premises that the 2MT odor promotes innate fear, but the behavioral characterization of the 2MT is very poor. The only information we have is supplementary Figure 1, with an example of the trajectories and the overall quantification of freezing.
a. The methods section lacks a description of how freezing is calculated. The authors only mention that it's done via software.
b. Regarding the methods, the authors mention six trials for each odor, but we always see only the averages of the six trials. Is there a desensitization/habituation to the odor? In addition, it's mentioned that there is a one-second exposure of the odor per trial, but there is no mention of how long the wait between trials is.
c. Do all mice display innate fear responses to the odor? Were mice excluded?
d. There is a critical inconsistency in the odor delivery protocols. The method section for the odor exposure to induce innate fear described for the fiber photometry are different from the one described in innate fear detection. More importantly, I could not find any information on how the odor is integrated with the pain assays in the manuscript. Is the odor delivered continuously while the pain assays (like von Frey test, Hargreave's test, etc) are ongoing? Are the mice exposed to it only once before initiating the battery of pain assays or at the beginning of each pain test? The timeline for the behavioural manipulations needs to be clarified.
All these points should be carefully addressed in order to understand the following figures of the manuscript and how exactly innate fear impacts pain sensitivity. This is particularly true since all the key readouts (e.g., increased thresholds, reduced nocifensive responses) may reflect motor suppression (freezing) rather than analgesia.
2. Although not clearly stated, the figures, figure caption and main text suggest that the same mice undergo the series of pain sensitivity tests for each experiment. For example, the same group of mice undergoes all the tests in the main figure 1. This suggests the authors rely on repeated pain testing in the same mice across multiple conditions without proper counterbalancing. This could lead to several problems. Stress-Induced Analgesia (SIA) is a well-documented phenomenon where repeated exposure to stress or pain itself alters subsequent sensitivity, and this could have a significant impact on the overall results and lead to possible confounds. There is no evidence that the pain sensitivity test exposure order was controlled, counterbalanced or test-order randomized. This weakens the overall conclusions of the manuscript.
3. The supplementary figure 6 Shows that modulation (particularly the inactivation) of APC GABA neurons regulates pain sensitivity without innate fear. This undermines the central claim that fear is required for analgesia. In response, the authors add Supplementary Figures 7 and 11, in which a comparison between the pain thresholds following neuronal inhibition with and without innate fear exposure is shown. However, these comparisons are convoluted, spread across multiple figures, and not clearly described. In detail:
a. Supplementary Figure 7 a-b - compared with supplementary figure 6 a-c with main figure 3 a-d
b. Supplementary Figure 7 c-d - compares supplementary figure 10 with main figure 5 a-d
c. Supplementary Figure 7 e-f - compares supplementary figure 11 a-c with main figure 6 a-d
d. And then, Supplementary Figure 11d-g relates to the main figure 6g-l
All of this back and forth is very chaotic and takes the attention away from the fact that there is a modulation of pain sensitivity alone, without the need for innate fear. Moreover, on the main text, the authors claim that these supplementary controls have "no significance differences" (line193-195;) and "did not show any differences in mechanical nociception (line 312-313)" and that is not true, which is simply incorrect based on the actual data of the supplementary figure. Moreover, the results of the thermal pain are not mentioned or compared. The data suggest that APC-GABA neurons modulate pain tonically and do not require fear for their effect. The manuscript selectively emphasizes data that support the fear angle and buries conflicting data in chaotic supplements.
4. No effort is made to dissociate freezing-induced motor suppression from true analgesic effects. Since 2MT induces freezing, reduced reactivity to pain stimuli could reflect behavioral suppression, not analgesia. The rotarod test is used to argue that circuit manipulations do not impair motor function. However, the rotarod primarily assesses gross motor coordination and balance, not fine motor output or spontaneous movement. - Paw withdrawal tests rely on quick reflex-like responses that may not be fully reflected in rotarod performance. Thus, motor slowing, freezing behavior, or motivational changes could still confound nociceptive assays.
5. The authors fail to adequately address the possibility that observed pain suppression results from inhibited motor output (such as freezing) rather than altered pain perception. The rotarod primarily assesses gross motor coordination and balance, not fine motor output or spontaneous movement. - Paw withdrawal tests rely on quick reflex-like responses that may not be fully reflected in rotarod performance. In addition, it seems that the activation of the APC-GABA promotes freezing in naive mice and decreases locomotion. Thus, motor slowing, freezing behavior, or motivational changes could still confound nociceptive assays. There can be a change in pain sensitivity merely because the manipulations impact motion.
6. In several key experiments (e.g., Fig. 2d: 3 mice; Fig. 2g–l: 5 mice per group), sample sizes are extremely small. The authors do not provide power analyses or variance estimates to justify these choices. How did the authors access the statistical power?
Minor points:
1. The introduction lacks referencing, e.g., lines 30, 32, 40, and 46.
2. The data referenced from lines 161 to 168 is not provided. It would be relevant to include such a dataset, yet only mechanical nociception is mentioned; thermal is missing.
3. Fig. 1b—The latency and number of licks or jumps are taken into consideration together, but there is massive variability. These are distinct behaviors and should be analyzed separately.
4. Fig. 1c - How is the % of response for the pinprick test calculated?
5. Fig. 2d - typo, the representative figure is panel c instead of d
6. Fig. 2g-l, heatmaps—not all animals seem to have a modulation of the neuronal activity during the delivery of 2MT. What could be the explanation?
7. Fig. 7 - Why, for physiological pain conditions, was only the thermal pain tested and not the mechanical?
8. Supplementary Figure 3 b-d - anisole group missing, therefore the conclusion on lines 120-121 that "These findings provide additional evidence for the involvement of APC neurons in processing fear-related olfactory information." could potentially be wrong since there is no odor that does not elicit fear responses.
9. Supplementary Figure 3g and j - only cotton swab. Airpuff is missing, and no explanation is provided for it to be the case.
10. Supplementary Figure 4 - The re-exposure to the arena should have been counterbalanced.
11. Supplementary Figure 9 and 11 - Typo, the letters associated with the panels are in CAPS.
The manuscript's conceptual framework offers an important mechanistic insight into how innate fear modulates pain sensitivity via an olfactory-cortical-thalamic GABAergic circuit. It is conceptually valuable and could contribute strongly to understanding how fear can suppress pain and lead to potential therapeutic targets for pain management. However, the current version of this manuscript contains significant interpretive overreach and methodological limitations. The central claim is not supported by the data as presented, and several key results are confounded. With substantial revision and reframing, the core finding—that an APC-GABA-MD circuit modulates pain sensitivity—could still represent a publishable advance, but not in its current conceptual framing as a fear-induced analgesia mechanism.

peer_review_rounds.author_response:
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful evaluation and constructive suggestions.
Major comments:
1. It is unclear that the manipulations are being done on a functionally relevant population. The cFOS in Figure 1 is quite different from the DREADD/mCherry expression for the recordings and manipulations in figure 2/3.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the difference between the cFOS patterns and the DREADD/mCherry expression. As shown in original Figure 1d, 2MT exposure activates both inhibitory and excitatory neurons, whereas in Figs. 2 and 3, the DREADD/mCherry experiments specifically target GABAergic neurons, which include a subset of Fos+ neurons. Thus, though partially overlapping, the two groups appeared to unidentical.
To directly address this concern, we now employed the TRAP2 strain, which enables genetic labeling and manipulation of neurons activated by a defined stimulation.1 To this end, we bilaterally injected AAV-VGAT-DIO-hM4Gi-mCherry into the APC of TRAP2 mice, followed by 2MT exposure paired with 4-OHT injection. Using this approach, we were able to specifically manipulate 2MT-activated inhibitory neurons. Inhibiting this ensemble significantly attenuated 2MT-induced fear expression and reduced 2MT-induced analgesia, but did not affect baselines thermal/mechanical nociception or locomotion (Response Fig. 1a-k; revised Fig. 4a-k). These findings establish that 2MT-responsive APCGABA neurons are necessary for innate fear-induced analgesia while being functionally distinct from basal nociceptive processing.
Furthermore, selective activation of 2MT-trapped APC inhibitory neurons was sufficient to evoke freezing and robust analgesia in the absence of 2MT, again without affecting motor performance (Response Fig. 1m-u; revised Fig. 4m-u). These complementary loss- and gain-of-function results demonstrate that 2MT-responsive APCGABA neurons are both necessary and sufficient for innate fear-related analgesia.
We have incorporated these data into the revised manuscript (lines 233-246; 275-282).
Response Fig 1. Chemogenetic manipulation of 2MT-activated inhibitory neurons in the APC.
a, l, Schematic of the viral injection and behavioral experimental timelines. b, m, Left: image of coronal section showing hM4Di (b) or hM3Dq (m) expression in APC. Right: the diffusion areas of viral expression at coronal level of APC. Subjects are individually colored (n=7). c, n, Effect of chemogenetically inhibiting (c) or activating (n) 2MT-TRAPed APCGABA neurons on the proportion of freezing time and total moving distance (n=7 mice/group). d, o, Baselines pain sensitivity following chemogenetic inhibition (d) or activation (o) of 2MT-TRAPed APCGABA neurons (n=7 mice/group). e, f, Effect of chemogenetically inhibiting 2MT-TRAPed APCGABA neurons on basal nociception (e) or chronic neuropathic pain (f) of 2MT-exposed mice (n=7 mice/group). g-k, q-u, Effect of chemogenetically inhibiting (g-k) or activating (q-u) 2MT-TRAPed APCGABA neurons on motor performance (n=7 mice/group). p, Effect of chemogenetically activating 2MT-TRAPed APCGABA neurons on neuropathic pain (n=7 mice/group). All data are presented as mean ± SEM except for the data in (b) depicted as box and whisker plots. “ns”, no significance; *p < 0.05, **p < 0.01. Significance was assessed by two-tailed paired Student’s t-test or Wilcoxon signed-rank test in (c, d, g-k, n, q-u), and two-way ANOVA followed by Bonferroni’s multiple comparisons test in (e, f, o, p).
2. The authors claim that inhibiting APC GABA neurons attenuates the effect of predator odor on pain and that activating APC GABA neurons recapitulates the effect of odor on pain. The data in the main and supplementary figures do not necessarily support this claim.
a. The activation of these neurons (hm3d and ChR2 experiments) should recapitulate what happens with the 2MT response. Figure 3 paints a far more complicated picture. Although, the authors state in the abstract “Conversely, activation of APCGABA neurons or the APCGABA-MD circuit recapitulates fear-induced analgesia.” This statement is not supported by figure 3 or 5.
We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful assessment of our claims regarding circuit recapitulation. We agree that our original abstract overstated the equivalence between natural 2MT responses and artificial activation paradigms. To more accurately reflect our findings, we have revised the statement to: “activation of APCGABA neurons or the APCGABA-MD circuit induces freezing responses and relieves pain, mimicking fear-induced analgesia” (lines 24-26).
b. APC GABA neuron inhibition affects pain independent of odor. The authors argue that because there was no significant difference between the inhibited groups with and without odor, the effect is not due to a change in baselines sensitivity. At face value this is confusing. First, this was only true for mechanical stimuli which was acknowledged but not discussed. Second, the authors should report the ANOVA interactions in Fig. S7 rather than comparing the two CNO groups. This would show if the effect of inhibition was different with and without 2MT, which I believe is the comparison the authors are trying to make.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful critique regarding the interpretation of our inhibition experiments.
The observation that basal nociception is affected by manipulation of APCᴳᴬᴮᴬ neurons indeed highlights the complexity of the interpretation. With TRAP2-based strategy to selectively target 2MT-responsive APC inhibitory neurons as presented above, we demonstrate that 2MT-responsive APCGABA neurons are both necessary and sufficient for innate fear-induced analgesia and are functionally distinct from those regulating basal nociceptive processing.
To streamlines the presentation and eliminate redundancy, we removed original supplementary Figure 7 and incorporated TRAP data into the revised manuscript (Revised Fig.4, lines 233-246; 275-282).
We thank the reviewer again for prompting these important improvements to our study's statistical rigor and interpretation.
c. The fact that only mechanical sensitivity seems to be further heightened by inhibition and the fact that activation produces analgesia even when predator odor is present (and presumably already activating APC neurons) makes it difficult to fully support the claim that this circuit underlies predator odor analgesia and not nociception in general. While it is important and appreciated that the authors showed the effects without odor (inhibition) and with odor (excitation), it would be helpful to explore the possibility that different manipulations might be able to better distinguish baselines nociceptive effects from odor.
i. Could the authors try changing their stimulation and inhibition parameters in a way that would not affect baselines thresholds but would still affect odor-induced analgesia?
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful suggestions regarding the distinction between baselines nociception and odor-specific effects. As suggested by the reviewer, we conducted optogenetic experiments testing new parameters using a reduced frequency (5 Hz). Unfortunately, we found that the 5Hz-stimulation alters the baselines pain thresholds as well (Response Fig. 3).
Response Fig 3. Effects of 5Hz-stimulation of APC-MD circuit on basal nociception.

Significance was assessed by two-tailed paired Student’s t-test in (b, d).
d. What proportion of APC GABA neurons are activated by 2MT? Is there subtype specificity that may be confounding the results? Would manipulating 2MT TRAPed APC inhibitory neurons more specifically affect predator odor analgesia and have less of an effect on baselines nociceptive thresholds?
We thank the reviewer for raising these important questions regarding molecular and functional specificity among APCGABA neurons. To address this, we quantified the proportion of APC GABA neurons that are activated by 2MT. Using traditional c-Fos staining, we found that ~40% of APC GABA neurons (Gad2) were Fos-positive after 2MT (Response Fig. 4, revised Fig. 12a-c).
As nicely suggested by the reviewer, we now specifically manipulated 2MT-TRAPed APC inhibitory neurons (Response Fig. 1; revised Fig. 4). In contrast to manipulating the entire APCGABA population, 2MT-trapped neural ensemble clearly dissociates odor-specific from general antinociception. We thank the reviewer again for this informative suggestion.
Response Fig 4. Quantification of proportion of APC GABA neurons that are activated by 2MT.
a, A cartoon illustrating c-Fos induction by 2MT exposure. b, c, Representative image (b) and summary data (c) for the percentage of GAD2-positive neurons (ISH, red) co-localized with c-Fos staining (blue) in the APC (n=15 sections from 5 mice). Scale bars, 500 μm and 50 μm. Data are presented as box and whisker plots (medians, quartiles (boxes), and ranges from minimum to maximum (whiskers)).
3. It is inappropriate to say that APC GABA neurons ‘encode’ fear-related olfactory information. Based on the data, the strongest conclusion that can be made is that they respond (transiently) to 2MT. Furthermore, the excitatory neurons in the APC also respond, making any conclusions about encoding more difficult.
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that our original wording overstated the interpretation. We have replaced “encode” with “respond to” or “are activated by” 2MT throughout the manuscript to more accurately reflect our findings.
4. There appears to be a mismatch between the neural activity recordings and the effect of this circuit on pain. How long were mice exposed to odors during the fiber photometry experiments? The neurons show clear bursts in activity, but the increase only lasts a few seconds. How could these neurons influence pain across minutes and hours? It would be beneficial to show neural responses during longer exposures that are similar to those the mice experience during behavioral tests.
a. Relatedly, there is some detail lacking in the results and methods sections on how mice were exposed to the odors during behavioral assays.
We thank the reviewer for this valuable comment and apologize for not providing sufficient methodological details in the original submission, which may have created the impression of a discrepancy between neural activity and behavioral effects.
During the fiber photometry experiments, odor stimuli were delivered via air puff or cotton swab presentation. Each odor was tested across six repeated trials with 1-minute inter-trial intervals. In each trial, mice were exposed to odors for 1 second. This transient delivery paradigm was optimized to capture the rapid temporal dynamics of population activity. In contrast, during behavioral assays, odors were continuously presented via filter paper near the testing arena to mimic sustained naturalistic exposure, which can engage downstream plasticity in regions such as the MD (Figs. 5-6) and mediate longer-lasting behavioral modulation.
In response to the reviewer's suggestion, we conducted additional fiber photometry recordings during prolonged odor exposure (20-min duration) under conditions similar to our behavioral assays. Our data demonstrated comparable APCGABA neural dynamics during odor zone visits between the initial 5-min phase and the terminal 5-min phase (Response Fig. 5), demonstrating persistent APCGABA activity throughout the exposure period. We have incorporated the above details regarding odor exposure during behavioral testing into both the Results and Methods sections (lines 153-154; 612-619; 684-690).
Response Figure 5. Similar APCGABA neural activity in initial vs. terminal 5-min of 20-min odor exposure
a, Schematic of viral injection and fiber implantation in VGAT-Cre mice (left) and a diagram of fiber photometry recordings triggered by entries into the odor zone containing 2MT (right). b, c, Heatmaps (b) and AUC analysis (c) showing Ca2+ transients upon entry into the 2MT zone during the initial and terminal five-minute periods. All data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. “ns”, no significance. Significance was assessed by two-tailed unpaired Student’s t-test in (c).
5. Figure 5G-I is confusing as presented and the claim based on these data are not currently fully supported. The authors claim that inhibition of APC GABA  MD, “2MT failed to rescue SNI-elicited MD hyperactivity…” (lines 299). At minimum, the authors should include mCherry and hM4 groups that were not exposed to 2MT to show the effect in controls and compare it to the effect after inhibition. It would also be helpful to include “SNI” and “2MT” in the labels of these panels and indicate that these data are from MD and not APC slices.
We thank the reviewer for the thoughtful critique of our MD thalamus electrophysiology data and agree that additional controls and clearer presentation are needed to support our conclusions.
In response, we performed additional patch clamp recordings from MD neurons in SNI mice expressing mCherry or hM4Di. We found that inhibition of MD-projecting APCGABA neurons did not further alter the SNI-induced MD hyperactivity, as measured by firing rate and rheobase, likely reflecting a ceiling effect of SNI-induced MD neural hyperactivity. Following 2MT treatment, MD hyperactivity was normalized in mCherry-expressing mice, but this rescue effect was abolished in hM4Di-expressing mice (Response Fig. 6, revised Fig. 6g, h).
We have also revised the figure presentation by adding “SNI” and “2MT” labels and explicitly indicating that the recordings were performed from MD, not APC, slices. These new data and clarifications have been incorporated into the revised manuscript (lines 363-376).
Response Fig 6. Inhibition of MD-projecting APC neurons attenuates 2MT-reversed MD hyperactivity in chronic pain.
a, b, Effects of the chemogenetic inhibition of MD-projecting APCGABA neurons on the firing rate (a) and rheobase (b) of MD neurons recorded from either water or 2MT-exposed SNI mice (DIO-hM4Di SNI&H O, n=18 neurons from 4 mice; DIO-mCherry SNI&H O, n=26 neurons from 4 mice; 2 2 DIO-hM4Di SNI&2MT, n=27 neurons from 3 mice; DIO-mCherry SNI&2MT, n=23 neurons from 3 mice). All data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.0001, not significant (ns).
6. While figure 5 (retro-cre) is not miswritten, there remains the caveat that these neurons could have collateral projections.
We thank the reviewer for this insightful comment. We agree that, while the retro-Cre approach effectively targets APC→MD projection neurons, it cannot exclude the possibility that these neurons possess collateral projections to other regions. We have now acknowledged this caveat in the revised discussion (lines 511–522). To address this limitation, our optogenetic experiments specifically manipulated the APC neural terminals within the MD and recapitulated the behavioral phenotypes observed during suppression of MD-presynaptic APCGABA neurons, demonstrating the functional specificity of this pathway.
7. Supplementary figure 9 kind of undercuts the story… a very small proportion of fos expressing neurons seem to project to the MD.
We thank the reviewer for this thoughtful observation. We fully acknowledge that the relatively small proportion of Fos⁺ neurons projecting to the MD thalamus, as shown in Supplementary Figure 9, warrants careful interpretation.
Methodologically, the limited overlap may partly stem from inherent constraints of retrograde tracing, as some activated MD-projecting neurons might not be labeled. Biologically, however, the high activation rate (~78%) within this subpopulation suggests functional specificity rather than weak circuit engagement. These findings indicate that, although numerically limited, a specialized subset of MD-projecting APCGABA neurons is preferentially recruited by 2MT and exerts a functionally significant influence on fear-related analgesia. We have clarified this point in the revised manuscript (lines 495–504).
8. As CamKII neurons were also activated, it is unclear why they were not functionally tested.
We appreciate this insightful question regarding the CaMKII-positive neurons in our study. We initially focused on GABAergic populations because 2MT elicited stronger and more selective calcium responses in inhibitory neurons, whereas excitatory neurons showed comparable activation to both 2MT and anisole (Fig. 2g-l). This specificity suggested a predominant role of APCGABA neurons in fear-induced analgesia.
In addition, when we manipulated the whole population of glutamatergic APC neurons by virally expressing DREADDs under the CaMKII promoter in wild-type mice, epileptic behavior was induced, precluding further behavioral testing (see attached supplementary video). Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Jia et al. provide an extensive assessment of the role of the anterior piriform cortex in mediating the analgesic effect of innate fear. The topic is highly interesting but complex as it is not easy to conceptually link the impact of innate fear on pain sensation. To do so the authors exposed mice to the odor of predators and then proceed to a battery of pain-related tests, showing that animals previously exposed to the odor predator exhibit reduced nocifensive behavioral responses. Using an extensive combination of anatomical, imaging, and functional approaches they progressively identify a GABAergic projections from the anterior proportion of the piriform cortex to the mediodorsal thalamus that may be both necessary and sufficient for this effect. This result calls for particular attention since long-distance inhibitory projections from cortex to the MD has never been reported before in mice. The amount of experimental work is impressive and all approaches are by themselves state-of-the-art, but the meaning and interpretation of all these experiments also appear as somewhat questionable. In addition, crucial methodological details are missing as explained below.
RESPONSE: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's thoughtful evaluation of our study and the important concerns. Below we provide point-by-point responses to strengthen the manuscript.
Methodology/behavioral paradigm
The exact protocol for odor exposure is not clear enough in relation with the many experiments reported. When exactly and for how long are animals exposed to the different odours? Is it acute or multiple exposures? Is it during each beahvioral assay or just before? Dpending on the answers to these questions there may be new issues to consider. Too many crucial details are lacking preventing the reader from understanding what exactly has been done.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the odor exposure protocol. We have now revised the Methods section to include detailed, step-by-step description of each procedure to ensure full experimental transparency:
• Pain behavior assays: Mice were first acclimated to the behavioral chamber for 30 minutes prior to testing. After acclimation, a continuous 2MT (or control solvent) odor was introduced by placing a filter paper saturated with the stimulus at the top of the chamber. Measurements of thermal or mechanical sensitivity (Hargreaves and von Frey tests) began 2 minutes after odor onset, and the odor stimulus was maintained throughout the entire testing session. This ensured that the animals remained in a sustained state of innate fear during nociceptive assessment.
• Odor-evoked calcium imaging: Mice were habituated for 30 minutes in a square testing box before odor presentation. Odor stimuli (water, anisole, or 2MT) were delivered either by air puff or cotton swab, with six repeated trials per odor and 1-minute inter-trial intervals. Each odor exposure lasted 1 second per trial. For delivery, a Pasteur pipette or cotton swab containing 50 μl of odor solution was briefly introduced into the chamber.
• Electrophysiology experiments: Mice received intraperitoneal CNO (30 minutes prior) to either 1-hour 2MT or water exposure, after which acute brain slices containing the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus were prepared for electrophysiological recordings.
We apologize for the lack of methodological details in the original submission. The revised manuscript now adds these procedures. The revised manuscript now includes these clarifications in the Methods section to facilitate reproducibility and interpretation of our findings.
For all histological controls, not enough data are provided to document the spread of viral infusion. For all interventions (DREADD and opto), general histology should be provided showing shades of spread for each included individual as is usually the norm.
Without these essential controls/information, the conceptual ground of the whole paper is unclear.
We thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of providing comprehensive histological documentation of viral spread. In the original study, viral expression was microscopically verified for all animals included in the analyses; however, we acknowledge that not all histological sections were documented photographically, and therefore, only a portion of the corresponding images is currently available. We have now compiled and included all existing histological images from these earlier cohorts in the revised submission (Response Figure 10). While these data represent only a subset of the DREADD and optogenetic experiments, they consistently show correct targeting and confinement of viral expression within the intended regions, supporting the reliability of our injection procedures.
To fully address the reviewer’s recommendation, we conducted a new, independently replicated chemogenetic experiment using TRAP2 mice, for which viral expression was systematically analyzed and documented for every individual animal. The revised supplementary Fig. 4 (Response Figure 11) now provides representative micrographs and schematic reconstructions for all subjects, aligned to standard brain atlas plates to clearly illustrate the extent and reproducibility of viral spread.
We acknowledge the limitation that complete photographic documentation of viral spread is not available for every animal from the earlier cohorts. Nonetheless, the consistency observed across the available images and the newly generated, fully quantified dataset together demonstrate that our viral manipulations were well targeted and reproducible, reinforcing the validity of the reported findings.

GABAergic projection from cortex to thalamus
The authors should really comment on whether this was expected or not. Very importantly, greater care is needed to ensure that this important claim is unambiguously supported by included data.
We thank the reviewer for this important point. The identification of a long-range GABAergic projection from the anterior piriform cortex (APC) to the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus was indeed unexpected, as the cortico-thalamic pathway is classically considered glutamatergic4,5. Based on the established findings regarding long-range cortical GABAergic projections (auditory cortex→lateral amygdala pathway6, and medial prefrontal cortex→to the retrosplenial cortex pathway7), our study provides evidence for the existence and functional significance of a GABAergic projection from the APC to the MD.
Specifically, our multidisciplinary approach combining viral tracing, optogenetics, chemogenetics and electrophysiological recordings provide the anatomical evidence of APC→MD inhibitory projection, and demonstrates crucial role of the APC→MD pathway in innate fear-induced analgesia.
The discovery of this APC→MD pathway aligns with the growing recognition of cortical long-range inhibitory circuits as important regulators of distant brain regions (such as amygdala and cortex)6,7. Our results extend this emerging paradigm to the olfactory system, revealing a previously uncharacterized inhibitory corticothalamic circuit that may coordinate cross-regional behavioral outputs during threat perception.
These points have been incorporated into the revised discussion (lines 486-487; 489-494).
For example, neurons that are positive for vgat may also transmit glutamate, how do we know if that is not the case here?
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. Indeed, a subset of VGAT-positive neurons has been reported to co-release glutamate under certain conditions. While the precise incidence of such co-transmission within the specific cortical population we targeted remains to be determined, evidence from the mouse cerebral cortex indicates that co-expression of VGAT and VGLUT1 at the synaptic level is rare, approximately 3.6 ± 0.2% of VGAT⁺ puncta8. Importantly, the net physiological effect of optogenetic activation in our study was pain suppression, a response that is inconsistent with predominant glutamatergic excitation. Thus, while we cannot completely exclude the possibility that a small subset of VGAT⁺ neurons may co-release glutamate, our functional and anatomical data strongly support that the observed effect is primarily mediated through GABAergic transmission. Future intersectional strategies selectively deleting glutamatergic signaling components in this population will help clarify any potential modulatory contribution of co-released glutamate to the observed fear-induced analgesia.
Viral spread into TRN which is mentionned in the paper is guaranteed to yield thalamic inhibition but this is not taken into consideration.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important concern. We fully agree that off-target viral expression in the thalamic reticular nucleus (TRN) could potentially confound the interpretation of our results by introducing unintended thalamic inhibition. As now documented in the Response Fig. 12, we confirmed that in the TRAP2 mice included in the final behavioral analyses, viral expression was largely restricted to the intended cortical target regions, with no detectable spread into the TRN.

The authors also reasonned that there is a higher proportion of GAD2+ proportion of cells labelled for dtomato than it is for CamKII cells (Figure 2c and 2d, the first d should be c though) but the panel c shows very few GAD2+ cells whereas CAMKII+ cells are abundant. This casts further doubt on that inhibitory CT route which would be further fraction at best of those GAD2+ cells (those projecting to the MD). All these issues add on each other, making the whole point not compelling given the importance of the claim.
We thank the reviewer for this comment and apologize for any lack of clarity in our original manuscript. The key point is not a direct comparison between the absolute proportions of GAD2+ and CaMKII+ cells within the tdTomato-labeled population.
It’s true that the absolute proportion of CaMKII+ cells within the tdTomato-labeled population is higher than GAD2+ cells. Rather, the critical finding is the differential change in these proportions between experimental groups (2MT versus anisole; 2MT versus H O). As we now state more clearly in the revised manuscript, upon 2MT 2 exposure, the proportion of GAD2+ cells among the tdTomato-labeled neurons significantly increased compared to the control groups. In contrast, the proportion of CaMKII+ cells remained unchanged. This specific, divergent response underscores that the fearful stimulus selectively recruits the inhibitory neurons, thereby validating their functional relevance.
Taken together, these issues largely undermine the paper to the extent that it is unclear whether the main points could still hold if they can be adequately addressed and making any more minor comments irrelevant at this stage. The paper would also benefit from professional level proof-reading for english.
We sincerely thank the reviewer for their thoughtful and constructive feedback, which has greatly strengthened the quality and clarity of our manuscript. Below, we summarize the major revisions made to address the concerns raised:
1) Expanded methodological details on odor exposure:
The Methods section has been substantially revised to provide step-by-step descriptions of odor presentation across all experimental paradigms. Detailed information is now included regarding the timing, duration, and delivery method of odor stimuli for behavioral assays, calcium imaging, and electrophysiological recordings, ensuring transparency and reproducibility.
2) Comprehensive histological validation of viral expression:
We performed detailed histological verification of viral expression in both the original and newly conducted experiments. All available histological images from earlier cohorts have been compiled, confirming accurate targeting of the anterior piriform APC. Additional chemogenetic experiments in TRAP2 mice were conducted, with viral expression systematically quantified and documented for each individual animal. These data show that viral expression was largely restricted to the APC, with minimal off-target spread.
We thank the reviewer for this stringent assessment and fully acknowledge that the initial submission lacked crucial methodological details and controls, which undermined the conceptual foundation of our study.
However, we fully acknowledge several limitations of the current study. The VGAT promoter-based viral system used to target GABAergic neurons in the APC may still carry off-target effects that cannot be completely excluded. It also remains to be determined whether a direct APCGLU-MD projection contributes to fear-induced analgesia. Given the known local feedback and feedforward inhibition within the piriform cortex9,10, further studies will be required to dissect the relative contributions of excitatory–inhibitory interactions within the APC and potential disynaptic pathways involving long-range excitatory activation of MD GABAergic neurons.
These considerations have been explicitly incorporated into the revised Discussion.
Finally, the entire manuscript has undergone comprehensive professional English editing to improve clarity, precision, and overall readability.

The manuscript by Jia et al. describes a very interesting set of findings revealing a potential circuit underlying pain suppression by innate fear. Of particular interest this is a novel long-range GABAergic projection originating from Anterior Piriform Cortex (APC) and targeting MD thalamus. Methodologically, the limited overlap may partly stem from inherent constraints of retrograde tracing, as some activated MD-projecting neurons might not be labeled. Biologically, however, the high activation rate within this subpopulation suggests functional specificity rather than weak circuit engagement. These findings indicate that, although numerically limited, a specialized subset of MD-projecting APCGABA neurons is preferentially recruited by 2MT and exerts a functionally significant influence on fear-related analgesia. Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript by Jia and colleagues, the authors investigate the neural mechanisms by which innate fear suppresses pain sensitivity in male mice, identifying a GABAergic projection from the anterior piriform cortex (APC) to the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) as a key component. Using a combination of viral tracing, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, chemogenetics, and optogenetics, the authors claim to show that innate fear—triggered by predator odor (2MT)—induces analgesia via this corticothalamic circuit.
While the study is methodologically rich and addresses an important topic, several conceptual, methodological, and interpretive issues significantly dampened the excitement about the manuscript and its current impact. The manuscript overstates its mechanistic conclusions. In my opinion, the core effects observed are better interpreted as modulations of pain sensitivity, rather than evidence of a distinct analgesic state induced by innate fear.
Major points:
1. The manuscript relies on the premises that the 2MT odor promotes innate fear, but the behavioral characterization of the 2MT is very poor. The only information we have is supplementary Figure 1, with an example of the trajectories and the overall quantification of freezing.
We thank the reviewer for this important critique regarding the behavioral characterization of 2MT-induced fear responses and agree that detailed behavioral validation is essential. 2MT is a well-established innate fear odor. This phenomenon has been extensively documented and replicated in multiple independent reports. In the revised manuscript, we now explicitly cite these foundational studies and clarify that our behavioral results (Supplementary Fig. 1) are consistent with this well-established literature11,12.

As pointed by the reviewer, the protocol used to induce innate fear in the Supplementary Fig. 1 was different from that used in photometry recordings. For 2MT-induced innate fear, mice were exposed to continuous 2MT odor delivery for 20 minutes to elicit robust freezing. A separate cohort of mice received six trials of 1-second 2MT exposure, with 1-minute inter-trial intervals. This design allowed us to isolate odor-evoked neural dynamics while minimizing olfactory adaptation.
For pain testing experiments, mice were first acclimatized to the behavioral chamber. Following an acclimatization period, a continuous 2MT (or control solvent) odor was initiated by placing a filter paper saturated with the stimulus at the top of the chamber. Pain assays (von Frey, Hargreaves, etc.) began 2 minutes after the onset of odor exposure, and the odor was maintained throughout the entire testing session to ensure animals remained in a sustained state of innate fear during nociceptive measurements.
We apologize for the lack of clarity in the original submission. The revised manuscript now includes a new Methods subsection titled “Timelines for Odor delivery” (lines 684-690), detailing these procedures.
All these points should be carefully addressed in order to understand the following figures of the manuscript and how exactly innate fear impacts pain sensitivity. We sincerely thank the reviewer for emphasizing the importance of clarifying how innate fear impacts pain sensitivity and for raising the possibility that reduced nocifensive responses could reflect motor suppression rather than true analgesia. We have taken several steps to address this concern comprehensively.
First, we have clarified all odor delivery protocols and experimental timelines to ensure that the relationship between innate fear and pain sensitivity is clearly understood in the context of each behavioral assay (see revised Methods section, “Timelines for odor delivery”).
Second, to dissociate motor suppression from analgesic effects, we performed additional analyses and fine motor behavioral assays (see responses to points 4 and 5). Quantification of locomotor activity during nociceptive testing showed no significant differences in movement or freezing levels between groups when mechanical or thermal stimuli were applied, indicating that changes in pain thresholds were not confounded by motor inhibition.
Third, our conditioned place aversion (CPA) and conditioned place preference (CPP) experiments provide direct behavioral evidence for genuine analgesia: activation of the APC-MD GABAergic circuit was reinforcing only under neuropathic pain conditions, not in naïve animals, supporting the interpretation that the observed behavioral changes reflect pain relief rather than motor suppression or reward.
2. Although not clearly stated, the figures, figure caption and main text suggest that the same mice undergo the series of pain sensitivity tests for each experiment. For example, the same group of mice undergoes all the tests in the main figure 1. This suggests the authors rely on repeated pain testing in the same mice across multiple conditions without proper counterbalancing. This could lead to several problems. Stress-Induced Analgesia (SIA) is a well-documented phenomenon where repeated exposure to stress or pain itself alters subsequent sensitivity, and this could have a significant impact on the overall results and lead to possible confounds. There is no evidence that the pain sensitivity test exposure order was controlled, counterbalanced or test-order randomized. This weakens the overall conclusions of the manuscript.
We thank the reviewer for this important comment and apologize for the ambiguous description of our behavioral tests paradigms. In the revised manuscript, we have clarified that separate cohorts of mice were used for the series of pain sensitivity tests shown in Figure 1. For experiments involving neural manipulations, pain sensitivity tests, from mild, basal nociception to post-injury assessments, were conducted in the same cohort of mice to allow within-subject comparisons under consistent physiological conditions.
As the reviewer correctly noted, repeated pain testing could potentially alter subsequent sensitivity through stress-induced analgesia (SIA) or test-order effects. To minimize these confounds, we employed a counterbalanced testing design in revision. In naïve C57BL/6 mice, four test modalities (von Frey, Hargreaves’, hot plate, and pinprick tests) were counterbalanced across animals. In nerve-injured and CFA-injected groups, two tests (von Frey and Hargreaves’) were counterbalanced (Response Fig. 19; revised Supplementary Fig. 10). Our analyses showed that baselines pain sensitivity remained stable across all test modalities regardless of order.
Importantly, the 2MT-induced analgesic effect was unaffected by testing sequence, confirming that test order did not influence our main conclusions.
We have incorporated these data into the revised manuscript (lines 208-219).

We sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s insightful critique regarding the interpretation of our inhibition experiments and agree that additional clarification is needed.
The observation that basal nociception is affected by manipulation of APCᴳᴬᴮᴬ neurons indeed highlights the complexity of the interpretation. Importantly, since only ~40% of APC GABA neurons are activated by 2MT (revised Supplementary Fig 12a-c), manipulating the whole APCGABA neuronal population could obscure odor-specific effects and confound the interpretation of fear-dependent analgesia.
To address this, we performed new experiments using a TRAP2-based strategy to selectively target 2MT-responsive APC inhibitory neurons. TRAP2 mice were bilaterally injected with either AAV-VGAT-DIO-hM4Di-mCherry or AAV-VGAT-DIO-mCherry into the APC, followed by 2MT exposure paired with 4-OHT injection. This approach enabled us to specifically manipulate the neuronal ensemble activated by 2MT. Chemogenetic inhibition of this 2MT-responsive ensemble attenuated both 2MT-induced fear expression and analgesia, without affecting baselines mechanical or thermal nociception or locomotor activity (Response Fig. 20a-k; revised Fig. 4a-k). Conversely, selective activation of this ensemble was sufficient to induce freezing behavior and robust analgesia even in the absence of 2MT, again without altering motor performance (Response Fig. 20m-u; revised Fig. 4m-u).
Together, these findings demonstrate that 2MT-responsive APCGABA neurons are both necessary and sufficient for innate fear–induced analgesia and are functionally distinct from those regulating basal nociceptive processing. We believe these experiments significantly strengthen our ability to distinguish general nociceptive effects from odor-specific modulation.
To streamlines the presentation and eliminate redundancy, we removed original supplementary Figure 7 and incorporated TRAP data into the revised manuscript (lines 233-246; 275-285).

4. No effort is made to dissociate freezing-induced motor suppression from true analgesic effects. Since 2MT induces freezing, reduced reactivity to pain stimuli could reflect behavioral suppression, not analgesia. The rotarod test is used to argue that circuit manipulations do not impair motor function. 5. The authors fail to adequately address the possibility that observed pain suppression results from inhibited motor output (such as freezing) rather than altered pain perception. The rotarod primarily assesses gross motor coordination and balance, not fine motor output or spontaneous movement. - Paw withdrawal tests rely on quick reflex-like responses that may not be fully reflected in rotarod performance. In addition, it seems that the activation of the APC-GABA promotes freezing in naive mice and decreases locomotion. Thus, motor slowing, freezing behavior, or motivational changes could still confound nociceptive assays. There can be a change in pain sensitivity merely because the manipulations impact motion.
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this crucial interpretive challenge. We agree that rotarod performance alone cannot exclude subtle motor impairments in fine motor output or motivational state. To rigorously dissociate true analgesic effects from motor suppression, we conducted a comprehensive battery of behavioral assessments evaluating both fine and gross motor functions.
First, to directly test whether 2MT-induced freezing impairs motor performance, we measured forelimb grip strength and found no significant difference between 2MT-exposed and water-exposed mice (Response Fig. 21a; revised Supplementary Fig. 2a). Next, high-speed paw kinematic analysis during the pinprick assay revealed comparable paw withdrawal velocities and amplitudes between groups (Response Fig. 21b; revised Supplementary Fig. 2b), indicating that 2MT exposure does not impair reflexive motor output.
We further assessed motor coordination and balance using the balance beam and rotarod tests. No differences were detected in traversal time (balance beam) or latency-to-fall (rotarod) between 2MT- and water-treated mice (Response Fig. 21c, d; revised Supplementary Fig. 2c, d). Together, these results demonstrate that the observed analgesic effects of 2MT are not attributable to motor impairment. We have incorporated these data into the revised manuscript (lines 97-111).
In experiments involving APC and APC–MD circuit manipulations, we applied the same battery of motor assessments and similarly found no evidence of motor suppression (Response Fig. 22; revised Supplementary Fig. 9), further confirming that the analgesic effects reflect altered pain perception rather than reduced motor output. We have incorporated these data into the revised manuscript (lines 203-205; 263-266; 350-352).
Importantly, our conditioned place aversion (CPA) and conditioned place preference (CPP) assays provide independent behavioral validation of true analgesia. For instance, inhibition of the APC-MD GABAergic pathway increased aversive responses, while its activation produced preference behavior only under neuropathic pain conditions, not in naïve animals (Revised Supplementary Fig. 16). This context-dependent reinforcement pattern supports the conclusion that APC-MD circuit activity alleviates pain rather than producing general reward or locomotor effects, further confirming that the observed reductions in nocifensive behaviors represent genuine analgesic outcomes.

The manuscript's conceptual framework offers an important mechanistic insight into how innate fear modulates pain sensitivity via an olfactory-cortical-thalamic GABAergic circuit. It is conceptually valuable and could contribute strongly to understanding how fear can suppress pain and lead to potential therapeutic targets for pain management. However, the current version of this manuscript contains significant interpretive overreach and methodological limitations. The central claim is not supported by the data as presented, and several key results are confounded. With substantial revision and reframing, the core finding—that an APC-GABA-MD circuit modulates pain sensitivity—could still represent a publishable advance, but not in its current conceptual framing as a fear-induced analgesia mechanism.
We are deeply grateful for the reviewer's insightful comments and constructive suggestions regarding the interpretation of our results and methodological limitations. In response to these important concerns, we have conducted a series of rigorous additional experiments:
We included new control experiments to systematically rule out potential confounding effects of motor suppression induced by 2MT or neural manipulation. We implemented comprehensive counterbalancing to test whether order effects in pain behavioral assessments exit. Importantly, through targeted manipulation of 2MT-activated APCGABA neuronal populations, we demonstrated no significant effect on baselines nociceptive thresholds, but selective modulation of 2MT-induced pain suppression. These new data substantially strengthen our conclusion that at least a distinct subpopulation of APCGABA neurons mediates fear-related pain suppression rather than general nociceptive processing.
In addition, we revised the title as “A corticothalamic circuit modulates pain sensitivity and mediates innate fear-induced analgesia in male mice”.
We believe these changes will address the reviewer’s concerns about overinterpretation while preserving the importance of identifying this previously unknown pathway in fear-pain interactions. We thank the reviewer for their suggestions that helped us improve the manuscript.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
I thank the authors for the important additional work performed to address some of the issues. The more detailed methodology and histology clearly add value to the paper.
I remain mildly concerned about how the existence of the long-distance inhibitory projection from APC to MD is contextualized. To the best of my knowledge, only one previous study has reported a similar pathway (Mazo et al., Nature Communications 2022). Although it was not the central claim of that paper and has not been widely cited, it should be acknowledged given the novelty of this finding. I hope this helps the authors appreciate the potential impact of their findings in the thalamocortical field specifically. A stronger effort to properly contextualize this result is still warranted.
Given the present evidence, the lack of converging data in the literature, and the relatively low number of such projecting GABA neurons (along with potential methodological caveats acknowledged by the authors), I believe the authors should adopt a careful and cautious tone in claiming the significance of this connection.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_5:
The revised manuscript by Jia et al. is much improved and strengthened. I appreciate the additional work that the authors have done to address my comments and those of the other reviewers. It's a substantial amount of work and that should be commendable. Overall, I'm more positive, however, one critical interpretational issue remains around locomotion/freezing confounds, and I believe one additional analysis is necessary to fully lock the interpretation.
The current supplementary Fig. 8 shows that activation of APC-GABA neurons increases freezing and decreases total distance. However, the manuscript (lines 263-264) still claims that "chemogenetic activation of APC GABA neurons did not affect motor performance, which was assessed by grip strength, high-speed paw kinematics, balance beam, rotarod, and OFT tests". This is inconsistent with the OFT result and should be corrected.
Similarly, in the new TRAP2 experiments (Fig. 4), the same is observed: inactivation leads to a decrease in freezing and activation leads to an increase in freezing and a decrease in the distance in the OFT. Given that these manipulations shift freezing/locomotion, any change in pain readouts could be secondary to general motor rather than pain modulation per se. The authors' added motor battery is useful but may not fully deconfound movement-dependent pain readouts.
Grip/beam/rotarod test capacity and coordination; Hargreaves, von Frey, hot plate, and pinprick still depend on movement thresholds and can be biased by freezing/locomotion.
I have two suggestions that should address this concern, are feasible, and will have a high impact.
1. Speed-/freezing-matched analyses.
Recompute the pain effects within bins of matched locomotor state (e.g., speed 0–1, 1–3, >3 cm/s; or "freezing" vs "non-freezing"). If analgesia persists in matched bins, that is strong evidence against a pure motor account.
2. Trial-by-trial mixed models with locomotion covariates.
Fit a GLMM/LMM: pain readout ~ manipulation + instantaneous speed + (manipulation×speed) + random intercepts per mouse.
- A significant manipulation main effect with small/NS interaction suggests locomotion does not explain it.
- Report effect sizes and partial R²
In the absence of these controls, the current data cannot exclude the possibility that pain changes are a consequence of altered freezing/locomotion rather than a modulation of nociception per se.
With these additions—and sustained, tempered wording that this pathway modulates pain and mediates a substantial component of odor-evoked analgesia—the work will be suitable for publication.

We thank the reviewer for this careful and insightful critique regarding the potential confounding influence of locomotor state on pain-related readouts. We agree that freezing and locomotion can, in principle, influence behavioral measurements and appreciate the thoughtful analytical suggestions.
In our study, standard reflexive nociceptive assays (von Frey, Hargreaves, pinprick) were performed under a widely accepted behavioral criterion: stimuli were delivered only when animals were stationary and the hindpaw was in a relaxed, weight-bearing position. Experimenters deliberately waited for periods of immobility prior to stimulus application to avoid confounding effects of voluntary movement on reflexive motor responses. Consequently, for all valid measurements, instantaneous locomotor speed at the time of testing was effectively zero by design, leaving no meaningful variance in locomotion to match across conditions or include as a covariate. For this reason, speed-matched binning and trial-by-trial mixed models incorporating locomotion are not applicable to these reflexive assays in our experimental framework.
That said, we fully agree that the proposed speed-matched and mixed-model approaches are highly appropriate for paradigms in which pain-related readouts are sampled continuously during free movement (e.g., measures of ongoing home-cage behavioral states, or decision-making tasks). We also acknowledge that, more broadly, for acute nociceptive responses measured using classical reflex-based assays, changes in freezing or locomotion can be difficult, and in many cases practically impossible, to fully deconfound. We have now explicitly added this limitation to the Discussion to clarify that altered motor state may influence the interpretation of certain reflexive pain measures as: “Finally, altered motor states like freezing can confound movement-dependent pain assessments. Therefore, integrating movement-independent readouts, such as facial grimace scales, will help to achieve a more comprehensive understanding of pain modulation by the APC→MD circuit.” (line 555-558).
To further address this concern, we also conducted Conditioned Place Aversion (CPA) and Conditioned Place Preference (CPP) assays in the manuscript, which assess the affective-motivational component of pain and do not rely on reflexive motor outputs. Importantly, during the test phase of CPA/CPP, animals freely explored the apparatus without neural manipulation, thereby eliminating acute effects on locomotion or freezing. Notably, the total distance traveled on the test day (Day 6) for CPP did not differ significantly between the hM3Dq and mCherry groups (Response Fig 1). We have now expanded the Discussion to clarify that measures of affective dimension of pain can help substantiate a modulation of nociception (line 475-479).
Response Fig 1. Total distance traveled during the CPP test phase.
a, Schematic of the conditioned place preference (CPP) experimental design. b, Quantification (left) and representative movement traces (right) of the total distance traveled during the CPP test phase (n = 5 mice per group). Data are presented as mean ± s.e.m. No significant difference (ns) was observed between groups.
Using these paradigms, APCGABA neurons or APC→MD circuit inhibition induced pain-associated aversion, whereas activation produced pain-relief-associated place preference. These results provide movement-independent evidence supporting a role of APCGABA neurons and APC→MD circuit in analgesia, particularly in the affective dimension of pain. Together, by clarifying the interpretational boundaries of reflexive nociceptive assays, our CPP/CPA results and discussion support the conclusion that APCGABA neurons or APC→MD circuit manipulation modulates pain and contributes substantially to odor-evoked analgesia.
Reference:
