## Methods

Animals. Adult (8–10 weeks) C57BL/6J, FosTRAP2, and Rosa26-tdTomato (Ai14) male mice were used in the experiments. C57BL/6J mice were purchased from Beijing Vital River Laboratory Animal Technology. CaMKII-Cre STOCK B6.Cg-Tg(Camk2a-cre)T29-1Stl/J (IMSR_JAX:005359), VGAT-Cre STOCK B6J.129S6(FVB)Slc32a1tm2(cre)Lowl/MwarJ (IMSR_JAX:028862), and Ai14 STOCK B6;129S6-Gt(ROSA)26Sortm14(CAGtdTomato)Hze/J (IMSR_JAX:007914) mice were initially purchased from Jackson Laboratories. FosTRAP2 STOCK Fostm2.1(icre/ERT2)Luo/J (Trap2) (IMSR_JAX:030323) mice were gifted by Dr. Shenbin Liu (Fudan University, China). To generate TRAP2::Ai14 mice for activity-dependent labeling experiments, FosTRAP2 mice were crossed with Ai14 mice. All mice were housed in groups of three to five mice per cage with free access to water and food in a biorhythm of 12 h light/12 h dark. The room temperature was kept at 23±1 °C and a consistent humidity of 50 ± 5%. All animal procedures and protocols were approved by the Animal Care and Use Committee of the University of Science and Technology of China.

Stereotaxic injection. The mice were administered intraperitoneal (i.p.) injections of pentobarbital sodium at a dosage of 20 mg/kg, and were then carefully positioned and adjusted on a stereotactic device (RWD Life Technologies Co., Ltd., China). To maintain the body temperature of the mice, a heating pad was utilized. Additionally, eye ointment was applied to protect the mice's eyes from any potential light irritation. A glass micropipette was utilized for injecting the viruses which are packaged and obtained by BrainVTA (Wuhan, China) in a volume of (300-320 nl for APC and 200-220 nl for MD) at a speed of 50 nl/min. After the injection, the micropipette was left in place for 10 minutes, allowing the virus to spread. Once the mice had recovered from the anesthesia, they were returned to home cages. Behavioral tests were performed 2-3 weeks later. The coordinates were defined as anterior-posterior (AP) from bregma, mediolateral (ML) from the midline, and dorsoventral (DV) from the brain surface (in mm).

Virus injection and optical fiber implantation. To manipulate APCGABA neurons, an adeno-associated virus (AAV) carrying the inhibitory hM4Di receptor under the control of the GABAergic neuron promoter (rAAV2/9-VGAT1-hM4D(Gi)-mCherry-WPRE-pA, 5.07E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0488) or the excitatory hM3Dq receptor (rAAV2/9-VGAT1-hM3D(Gq)-mCherry-WPRE-pA, 5.44E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0489) or rAAV2/9-VGAT1-mCherry-WPRE-pA (5.36E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0325) as control were injected into the APC (AP, +0.75 mm; ML, ± 3.25 mm; DV, -5.2 mm) bilaterally.

To inhibit MD-projecting APCGABA neurons, rAAV2/Retro-hSyn-CRE-WPRE-hGH-pA (5.22E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-2334) was injected into the MD (AP, -1 mm; ML, ±0.5 mm; DV, -3.3 mm) of C57 mice bilaterally, and rAAV2/9-VGAT1-DIO-hM4D(Gi)-mCherry-WPRE-hGH-pA (5.02E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0618) or rAAV2/9-VGAT1-DIO-mCherry-WPRE-hGH-pA (5.79E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-3225) was injected into the APC bilaterally.

To optogenetically manipulate APCGABA terminals within the MD, rAAV2/9-VGAT1-eNpHR3.0-EYFP-WPRE-hGH-pA (5.00E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0182) or rAAV2/9-VGAT1-hChR2(H134R)-mCherry-WPRE-hGH-pA (5.66E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0643) were injected into the APC bilaterally. rAAV2/9-VGAT1-EYFP-WPRE-hGH-pA (5.33E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0190) or rAAV2/9-VGAT1-mCherry-WPRE-pA (5.44E+12 vg/ml) was used as controls.

To verify the specificity of the VGAT-promoter driven viruses, we injected a mixture of rAAV2/9-DIO-EYFP (5.14E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0012) and rAAV2/9-VGAT1-mCherry-WPRE-pA viruses (1:1) into the bilateral APC of VGAT-Cre mice.

Fiber photometry. To assess calcium changes, rAAV2/9-hSyn-GCaMp6m-WPRE-hGH-pA (300 nl, 5.14E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0148), rAAV2/9-VGAT1-GCaMp6m-WPRE-hGH-pA (300 nl, 5.79E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-3317), or rAAV2/9-CaMKIIa-GCaMp6m-WPRE-hGH-pA (300 nl, 5.04E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0111) was injected into the APC (AP, +0.75 mm; ML, -3.25 mm; DV, -5.2 mm) unilaterally in C57 mice. Additionally, rAAV2/9-DIO-GCaMP6m-WPRE-pA (300 nl, 6.21E+12 vg/ml, Cat. No. PT-0283) was injected into the APC of VGAT-Cre or CaMKII-Cre mice. Two weeks later, the optical fiber (diameter: 200 μm; N.A.: 0.37; length: 5.5 mm; Inper, China) was embedded at the APC by attaching dental cement to the skull. After a one-week recovery, Ca2+ signals of APC were recorded by the three-color single-channel fiber photometry system (ThinkerTech, China).

Mice were initially placed in a square box and allowed habituation for 30 minutes. During the fiber photometry experiments, odor stimuli—including water, anisole (Sigma, Cat. No. 296295), and 2MT (Tokyo Chemical Industry, Cat. No. M0285) were presented via air puff or cotton swab. Each odor was tested across six repeated trials with 1-minute inter-trial intervals. In each trial, mice were exposed to the odor for 1 second. For air-puff or cotton swab delivery, a Pasteur pipette or a cotton swab containing 50 μl of the odor solution was manually introduced into the chamber for 1 second. By clicking the Mark button on the software (ThinkerTech, China) at the moment when the odorant stimuli were delivered, the behavioral and fluorescent events could be time-locked. The fluorescence signal of each mouse was analyzed six times.

Neurons and terminals expressing GCaMP6m were stimulated by laser intensity at 470 nm wavelength (40 μW) to obtain calcium-dependent fluorescence signals, while motion artifacts were corrected by laser signal at 410 nm (20 μW). The obtained calcium signal was analyzed by MATLAB software and calculated (F−F0)/ F0 (average baseline fluorescence signal) to calculate the changed value of the Ca2+ signal (ΔF/F). The 5-second window around the event was analyzed, using a 2-second window before the stimulus as the baseline. The result was the averaged data from the first six Ca2+ responses (six trials) of each mouse.

Optogenetic manipulation. To optogenetically manipulate APCGABA terminals within the MD, two weeks after the bilateral virus injection into the APC, the optical fibers (diameter: 200 μm; N.A.: 0.37; length: 4.0 mm; Inper, China) were embedded at the MD by attaching dental cement to the skull bilaterally. One week later, behavioral tests were performed. In experiments, the optical fiber in the mice's heads was connected to the laser source through a sleeve line.

For optogenetic manipulation, the intensity of the blue light (473 nm, 2.5 mW, 10 ms, 20 Hz) or the yellow light (594 nm, 5 mW, 10 ms, 20 Hz) was measured and determined by the photometer and then controlled by the device (QAXK-LASER, ThinkerTech, China). On the first day, mice had their heads interfaced with the laser system but were not exposed to any light stimuli. The following day, they underwent distinct exposures to either blue or yellow light stimuli to observe differences in behavioral phenotypes. Mice in the control virus groups had the same stimulation regimen.

In detail, during the entire pain experiment, we initially exposed the neurons or circuits to light for 1 minute to enable control. Following this, we employed a stimulation regimen of 1 minute ON and 5 minutes OFF to assess mechanical and thermal sensitivity. During the ON phase, we conducted the necessary measurements. Afterward, the mice were given a 5-minute rest before we repeated the aforementioned steps. For the hot plate test, we used the 3 minutes ON and 5 minutes OFF stimulation regimen.

Chemogenetic manipulation. To manipulate the activity of specific neurons, mice expressing chemogenetic viruses were intraperitoneally injected with CNO (2 mg/kg, APExBIO Technology LLC, Cat. No. A3317) prior to the experiment. After a period of 30 minutes, during which the drug became effective, behavioral experiments were conducted. In the actual experimental procedure, mice are initially administered saline intraperitoneally on the first day to assess their behavioral phenotypes. On the following day, CNO is injected intraperitoneally into the mice to evaluate any differential behavioral phenotypes.

Innate fear detection. In experiments to test the fear, the proportion of the freezing time, the movement distance, and the behavior adjacent to the odor were chosen as indicators to detect fear. To conduct these experiments, the mice were placed in a square glass box lined with clean filter paper. The mice were allowed to acclimate to the apparatus for 30 minutes the day before the innate fear-associated experiments. On the day of the experiment, the mice were initially placed in the box to explore freely for 10 minutes. Then, either water (20 μl), anisole (20 μl), or 2MT (20 μl) was dropped onto the upper left corner of the filter paper using a pipette. The mice were then exposed to the specific odor for 20 minutes. Finally, the proportion of the freezing time and the movement distance, including the trajectory of the mice within the 20-minute period, were analyzed using software (SuperFcs system, XinRuan, Shanghai, China). For data analysis, we utilized the built-in SuperMaze animal behavior video analysis software, Version 2.0. This software allowed us to adjust the Mobility/Immobility threshold to accurately differentiate between the mobility and immobility states of the mice, as well as modify the Immobility/Freezing threshold to effectively distinguish between immobility and freezing states induced by fear.

After conducting multiple tests, we determined the optimal initial values displayed on the software to be a Mobility/Immobility threshold of 16 and an Immobility/Freezing threshold of 19. Subsequently, we proceeded with the formal experiment. In all freezing-related experiments mentioned in this article, these preset threshold values were consistently used for analysis.

Certain experiments include the quantification of metrics, including the duration of residence in the odor zone and the number of entries into that zone, all of which are processed using SMART V3.0 software.

Timeline for odor delivery. For pain testing experiments, mice were first acclimatized to the behavioral chamber. Following an acclimatization period, a continuous 2MT (or control solvent) odor was initiated by placing a filter paper saturated with the stimulus at the top of the chamber. Pain assays (von Frey, Hargreaves, etc.) began 2 minutes after the onset of odor exposure, and the odor was maintained throughout the entire testing session to ensure animals remained in a sustained state of innate fear during nociceptive measurements.

Complete Freund's adjuvant (CFA) model. To induce chronic inflammation, CFA (10 μl, Sigma, Cat. No. 8. 18752) was injected into the hind paws of the mice. After a period of seven days following the injection, the withdrawal threshold was measured using the von Frey test, while the withdrawal latency was measured using Hargreaves’ test. In order to establish a baseline for comparison, mice that received an injection of saline (0.9% NaCl) were used as control subjects.

Spared nerve injury (SNI) model. Mice were anesthetized under the intraperitoneal injection of pentobarbital sodium (20 mg/kg) and then subjected to nerve injury or sham surgery. The skin on the lateral surface of the thigh was cut, and the sciatic nerve was exposed by separating the muscle with a glass minute needle. The common peroneal nerve and tibial nerve were separated from the sural nerve and ligated with nonabsorbent 4-0 chromic gut sutures (Ethicon), and the nerve 2-4 mm distal to the ligation site was resected. In the sham operation, the sciatic nerve and its three branches were exposed, but the nerve was not ligated. Fourteen days after surgery, the withdrawal threshold and withdrawal latency were measured by the von Frey test and Hargreaves’ test, respectively.

Inflammatory pain measurement (Formalin test). Mice were placed in a square glass box and allowed to acclimate for 10 minutes. A solution of formalin (10%, Xinhongfu Biotechnology) was prepared, which was then diluted to a 1% concentration using normal saline. Subsequently, the diluted solution (50 μl) was injected subcutaneously into the hind paw of each mouse The licking behavior of the mice was then videotaped with a camera immediately after injection. The number of licking episodes in one hour was recorded. The experiment was divided into two phases. The first phase, known as the acute phase, is comprised of the initial ten minutes. The second phase, referred to as the inflammatory phase, consisted of the remaining 50 minutes.

Mechanical sensitivity measurement (von Frey test). On the day of the behavioral experiment, the mice were initially acclimated to the plexiglass chambers (6.5 x 6.5 x 6 cm) and placed on a wire mesh for one hour. The Up-Down method was employed for the experiment75. Briefly, a series of von Frey filaments (North Coast Medical Inc., USA) were used to stimulate the plantar area of the hind paw for a duration of 3 seconds. The responses of the mice to each monofilament were recorded. Each monofilament was tested five times. There was a minimum interval of 5 minutes between each measurement. The stimulus strength that produced a 50% response rate was determined and taken as the withdrawal threshold.

Thermal sensitivity measurement (Hargreaves’ test). On the day of the behavioral experiment, the mice were initially given a one-hour period to acclimate to the plexiglass chambers, which measured 6.5 x 6.5 x 6 cm, on the Hargreaves’ Apparatus (IITC Life Science Inc., CA, USA). During the experiment, a radiant heat beam emitted by the machine was focused on the hind paws of the mice. Each mouse was subjected to a total of five exposures to the radiant heat beam, and the incubation period of paw withdrawal was carefully recorded. To ensure accurate data, there was a minimum interval of 10 minutes between each experiment. In order to prevent tissue damage and minimize the potential for pain sensitization, the duration of the radiant heat beam exposure was limited to a maximum of 20 seconds.

Acute thermal pain measurement (Hot plate test). The mice were placed on a hot plate (IITC Life Science Inc., CA, USA) at a temperature of 47 °C, and both the latency (time taken to respond) and episodes of nocifensive responses (such as jumping and licking) were carefully recorded. To avoid potential tissue damage, the duration of the 47 °C hot plate test was limited to 3 minutes. The control group was exposed to a temperature of 25 °C.

Acute mechanical pain measurement (Pinprick Test). The hind paw of the mice was gently stimulated ten times with a blunt needle that wouldn’t pierce or injure the skin. There was at least a one-minute interval between the each stimulation. The number of paw withdrawal reactions was recorded during these ten experiments, and the percentage of reactions was calculated as: (number of paw lifts)/(total trials [n=10]) × 100%.

Rotarod Test. Mice were tested on an accelerated rotary rod (IITC Life Science Inc., CA, USA). The training phase spanned the first two days, during which the mice were trained to maintain balance. The starting speed at 5 rounds per minute, gradually reaching a maximum speed of 20, and the duration of each training session was 5 minutes. On the third day, the test phase began, with the starting speed set at 5 and the maximum speed set to 40. The experimental duration was 5 minutes, during which the instrument automatically recorded the time it took for the mice to drop. The experiment was repeated twice, and the average value was calculated.

Balance beam. The balance beam test was performed using a 1-meter-long beam with a 12 mm wide flat surface, positioned 50 cm above the bench and supported by two rods. A black box containing nesting material from the home cage was placed at the far end of the beam to serve as an incentive. Mice were acclimatized to the apparatus for at least two days prior to testing. A refresher training session was conducted approximately 10 minutes before the formal test. If a mouse stalled, sniffed, or failed to advance, it was gently encouraged from behind using a gloved finger. It is worth noting that overtraining could increase stalling behavior due to overfamiliarity with the task. Conversely, mice that failed to traverse the beam after two training days received additional training. Once a mouse entered the black box, it remained there for approximately 15 seconds before the next trial. On the test day, the time taken to cross the beam (s) was recorded for each animal. The apparatus was cleaned with water and 75% ethanol after each trial to remove urine and feces.

Withdrawal kinetics. Withdrawal kinetics were assessed by applying gentle mechanical stimulation to the mouse hind paw using a blunt needle that did not puncture the skin. The response was recorded with slow-motion video, and the maximum vertical distance (mm) the stimulated paw was lifted from the ground was measured. The time (s) from initial lift-off to the highest point of withdrawal was also recorded. Based on these parameters, the paw withdrawal velocity (mm/s) was calculated. Three trials were conducted per mouse, and the average value was determined.

Grip strength. Grip strength was assessed using a grip strength meter (BIOSEB, EB Instruments). Each mouse was positioned on a metal grid and allowed to stabilize. The tail was then gently and steadily pulled backward along the plane of the grid until all four limbs were completely released. The peak grip force (g) displayed on the device was recorded. Sixteen consecutive trials were performed per animal, and the mean grip strength was calculated based on the last 12 trials (trials 5–16).

Conditional place avoidance and preference (CPA/CPP) test. The experimental setup consisted of two chambers with distinct visual cues: one chamber had black walls with black ground, while the other chamber had white walls with white ground. There was also a neutral middle area between the two chambers. The mice were allowed to move freely between the chambers, and their positions were recorded using an overhead camera. On the first day of the experiment, mice were acclimated to the device for 30 minutes, allowing the mice to familiarize themselves with the chambers and the visual cues. On day 2, the mice were given a 10-minute period to freely explore the entire device. During this exploration period, the time spent by each mouse in each chamber was recorded.

On days 3, 4, and 5, the mice underwent training sessions. For the CPA test, mice were placed in the white box with no light or saline injection for a duration of 30 minutes on the morning of the training day. Four hours later, mice were placed in the black box and were exposed to either yellow light stimulation or received an injection of CNO. For the CPP test, mice were kept in the black box with no light or saline injection. Four hours later, mice were placed in the white box and were subjected to blue light stimulation or CNO injection.

On day 6, mice were once again given a 10-minute period to freely explore the entire apparatus, and the time they spent in each chamber was recorded. The changes in position preference of mice before and after training were analyzed.

Activity-dependent Fos induction by innate fear. 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-OHT, Sigma, Cat. No. H6278) was dissolved in ethanol at a concentration of 20 mg/mL and shaken at 37 °C for 15 minutes, after which the solution was aliquoted and stored at -20 °C. Before use, 4-OHT was re-dissolved in ethanol by shaking at 37 °C for 15 minutes, followed by the addition of corn oil to obtain a final 4-OHT concentration of 10 mg/mL. Finally, the ethanol was removed by vacuum evaporation through centrifugation prior to use.

To label neurons specifically activated by innate fear odor 2MT, mice were housed individually before the odor exposure experiment. On the day of the experiment, 2MT solution (20 μl) was applied to filter papers, with H2O (20 μl) or anisole (20 μl) used for the control group. These filter papers were then placed in the cages for 1.5 hours. Subsequently, the mice received an intraperitoneal injection of 4-OHT at a dosage of 50 mg/kg in a final concentration of 10 mg/ml and were exposed to 2MT for an additional 1.5 hours. One week later, the brains of these mice were harvested for further analysis.

For the 2MT re-exposure experiment, TRAP2::Ai14 mice were acclimated to the experimental environment for two days prior to the initial exposure. On the day of the first exposure, the mice were exposed to 2MT (20 μL) for a duration of 3 hours. At 1.5 hours after the start of this exposure, 4-OHT (50 mg/kg) was administered by intraperitoneal injection. One week later, the re-exposure experiment was conducted, with the mice again being adapted to the environment for two days beforehand. During this re-exposure experiment, one group of mice received 2MT (20 μL) and another group received anisole (20 μL) for a period of 3 hours. Following the completion of the odor exposure, the brains were perfused for c-Fos staining.

Immunofluorescence and imaging. Mice were deeply anesthetized with isoflurane and perfused transcardially with 0.1 M PBS (phosphate-buffered saline) followed by PFA (4% paraformaldehyde). Dissected brain tissues were fixed in 4% PFA for an overnight period and then transferred to the sucrose (30%) at 4 °C. After the brains were dehydrated completely by sinking in sucrose, the brains were frozen in Tissue-Tek O.C.T (From SAKURA) and sectioned coronally (35 μm) with the freezing microtome (Leica CM1950, Leica Biosystems). The obtained sections were washed three times with PBS (at least five minutes each) and then incubated with blocking buffer (10% sheep serum in PBS plus 0.3% Triton X-100 in PBS) for one hour at room temperature. Brain sections were incubated with primary antibodies (Rabbit anti-GABA, 1:500, Sigma, Cat. No. A2052; Rabbit anti-c-Fos, 1:500, Synaptic Systems, Cat. No. 226 003) in the blocking buffer overnight at 4 °C. After washing three times with PBS the next day, brain sections were incubated with secondary antibodies (Goat anti-rabbit Alexa Fluor 488, 1:1000, Jackson, Cat. No. 111-545-003) for two hours in the blocking buffer. In the end, the sections were washed again three times with PBS, and then stained with DAPI, washed, mounted, and sealed after dropping anti-fluorescence quench. Immunostained brain sections were subjected to acquisition imaging using the Olympus FV3000 microscope.

Images obtained by laser confocal microscopy were analyzed using Image J or Adobe Photoshop. To quantify the cell proportion of c-Fos positive neurons or anti-GABA-positive neurons in the PC, three to five randomly selected brain sections were chosen for analysis. Dual-color fluorescence was quantified as above. The final percentage for each result was the average percentage of slices in each mouse.

Fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH). On the first day, brain slices are washed in DEPC-PBS for 5 minutes, followed by a 5-minute wash in DEPC-PTW (0.1% Tween-20 in PBS), and then incubated in 2x SSC + 0.5% Triton X-100 for 30 minutes. This is followed by two 5-minute washes in DEPC-PTW, after which the slices are incubated in 3% hydrogen peroxide-methanol for 10 minutes to block endogenous peroxidase activity, and then washed twice for 5 minutes in DEPC-PBS. The tissues are then incubated for 10 minutes in triethanolamine-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) containing 0.25% acetic anhydride without ribonuclease to acetylate free amines, followed by three 5-minute washes in DEPC-PBS. The tissue is prehybridized in prehybridization buffer (50% formamide, 25% 2x SSC, 0.3 mg/ml yeast RNA, 0.1 mg/ml heparin, 1x Denhardt’s solution, 0.1% Tween-20, 5 mM EDTA) for 2 hours at room temperature, before hybridizing with digoxigenin-labeled antisense cRNA probes for CAMKPII (873 bp amplified by primers AGTCTCCAAGCCAACCCC and ATAGAGNCGCACACCAGGC from NM_009792.1) and GAD2 (869 bp amplified by primers TCTTTTCTCCTGGTGGCG and AAATCTTGTCCGAGGCGTTCG from NM_008078.1) for 20 hours at 65 °C in the same buffer.

On the second day, the brain slices undergo a 30-minute wash in preheated (65 °C) prehybridization buffer, followed by a 30-minute wash in a 1:1 mixture of preheated (65 °C) prehybridization buffer and TBST. Next, there are two 5-minute washes in TBST, a brief wash in a 1:1 mixture of TBST and TAE, and three 5-minute washes in TAE. Unbound probes are removed by electrophoresis at 60V for 2 hours in a 2% agarose gel, after which the tissue is incubated overnight at 4 °C for 36 hours in Anti-Digoxigenin-POD antibody (Roche, Cat. No. 11207733910), diluted 1:1000 in PBT supplemented with 10% sheep serum.

On the third day, the brain slices are washed three times in TNT buffer, each for 10 minutes, and incubated with anti-IF 488 antibody (Servicebio, Cat. No. G1231), diluted 1:1000 in TBST containing 3% H2O2, for 20 minutes at room temperature, followed by immunofluorescence staining using antibodies against Chk pAb to mCherry (1:1000, abcam, Cat. No. ab205402) and Goat pAb to Chk IgY labeled with Alexa Fluor 594 (1:500, abcam, Cat. No. ab150172).

Brain slice electrophysiology. Mice were anaesthetized with isoflurane and then perfused with ice-cold oxygenated N-Methyl-D-glucamine (NMDG) artificial cerebrospinal fluid (ACSF) (20 mL) that contained (in mM): KCl (2.5), NMDG (93), NaHCO₃ (30), NaH₂PO₄ (1.2), glucose (25), HEPES (20), thiourea (2), Na-pyruvate (3), CaCl₂ (0.5), Na-ascorbate (5), MgSO₄ (10), and glutathione (3) (pH 7.3-7.4, 300-305 mOsm). Coronal slices (300 μm thickness) were then removed to ice-cold oxygenated NMDG-ACSF and sectioned on a vibrating microtome (VT1200s, Leica). The brain slices were transferred to oxygenated NMDG-ACSF at 32 °C for incubation and recovery, followed by oxygenated N-2-hydroxyethylpiperazine-N-2-ethanesulfonic acid (HEPES) ACSF that contained (in mM) 92 NaCl, 2.5 KCl, 1.2 NaH2PO4, 30 NaHCO3, 20 HEPES, 25 glucose, 3 Na-pyruvate, 5 Na-ascorbate, 2 thiourea, 2 CaCl2, 2 MgSO4 and 3 GSH (PH 7.3-7.4, 300-305 mOsm) for more than 1 h at 25 °C. Whole-cell patch-clamp recordings were performed in oxygenated standard ACSF that contained (in mM) 129 NaCl, 1.2 KH2PO4, 3 KCl, 2.4 CaCl2, 3 HEPES, 1.3 MgSO4, 10 glucose, and 20 NaNHCO3 (PH 7.3-7.4, 300-310 mOsm, oxygenated with 95% O2 and 5% CO2) at 25 °C.

Patch-clamp electrophysiology data were acquired with a MultiClamp 700B amplifier (Molecular Devices) and Clampfit pClamp 10.0 software. Signals were low-pass filtered at 2 kHz and digitized at 5 kHz using Digidata 1550B (Molecular Devices). The pipette (6-8 MΩ) was pulled by a micropipette puller (P-1000, Sutter instrument) and filled with the internal solution that contained (in mM): 130 K-gluconate, 5 KCl, 4 Na2ATP, 0.5 NaGTP, 20 HEPES, 0.5 EGTA (PH 7.28, 290-300 mOsm). To record an input-output curve of neuronal excitability, 10 pA command current steps with 500 ms pulses were injected from 0 to +150 pA, and the number of action potentials (APs) was quantified for each step. To confirm the efficacy of hM4Di-mediated inhibition and hM3Dq-mediated excitation, CNO (10 μM) was bath-applied. Optical stimulation was delivered using a laser through an optical fiber 200 μm in diameter positioned 0.2 mm from the surface of the brain slice. To confirm the efficacy of ChR2-mediated activation, fluorescently labeled neurons were stimulated with a 473 nm laser using 20 Hz stimulation protocols with a pulse width of 10 ms. In similar, the functional expression of eNpHR3.0 was assessed by applying yellow (594 nm) laser light stimulation.

To examine functional inhibitory projections from the APC to the downstream regions and sIPSCs of MD neurons, recordings were conducted in the presence of CNQX (10 μM, Sigma) and patch pipettes were filled with the chloride-based internal solution that contained (in mM): 145 CsCl, 10 EGTA, 10 HEPES, 2 MgCl2, 2 CaCl2, 2 Mg-ATP and 5 QX-314. Neurons were held at −70 mV using the voltage clamp for recording inward Cs+-IPSCs. For evaluating synaptic identities, GABA-mediated IPSCs were blocked by the bath application of bicuculline (10 μM, Sigma, Cat. No. 14343). To test direct synaptic connections, both TTX (1 μM, Sigma, Cat. No. A0224) and 4-AP (500 μM, Sigma, Cat. No. 275875) were used to restore monosynaptic current.

To investigate the effect of 2MT exposure on neuronal excitability, mice were placed in a cage containing 2MT for 1 hour prior to the experiment. Subsequently, they were sacrificed for brain slicing to ensure the sustained effect of the 2MT odor.

To investigate the effect of odor exposure on neuronal excitability, mice were continuously exposed to 2MT or water for 60 minutes by applying 20 μl odorant solutions to filter paper positioned at the testing arena. Acute brain slices containing the MD thalamus were then prepared for electrophysiological recordings.

To investigate the effect of chemogenetic inhibition on neuronal excitability, mice received intraperitoneal CNO injections (30 minutes prior) to either 1-hour 2MT or water exposure, after which acute brain slices containing the MD thalamus were prepared for electrophysiological recordings.

Quantification and statistical analysis. All experiments and data analyses were performed in a double-blind manner. GraphPad Prism v.8.0.1, Olympus FV10-ASW 4.0a Viewer, ImageJ, Clampfit software v.10.0, SuperFcs system, SMART V3.0 software, and MATLAB R2017b software were used to analyze the data. Unpaired Student’s t-test (or Mann-Whitney U test), paired Student’s t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank test), and one-way ANOVA or two-way ANOVA test followed by Bonferroni’s test for multiple comparisons were used to determine statistical differences. Shapiro-Wilk test was used to test whether the data followed a normal distribution. When data were normally distributed, paired and unpaired t-tests were implemented. When data did not conform to a normal distribution, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test was used for paired comparisons, while the Mann-Whitney U test was used for unpaired comparisons. Results with *P < 0.05, **P < 0.01, ***P < 0.001, ****P < 0.0001 were statistically significant. All data were presented as the mean ± s.e.m except for Supplementary Fig. 6 and 12 shown as box and whisker plots (medians, quartiles (boxes), and ranges from minimum to maximum (whiskers)). Detailed analysis results are shown in Supplementary Data 1.

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This study by Jia et al. examines the intersection between innate fear and pain. They start by characterizing how an innately fear-inducing odor affects pain across multiple modalities and timescales. 2MT induced analgesia in naïve animals as well as attenuated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in models of chronic pain. Figure 1 is quite a nice behavioral demonstration. The authors then perform experiments and reach the conclusion that GABAergic neurons in the anterior piriform cortex are activated by 2MT and that activating or inhibiting these neurons or their projections to the medial dorsal thalamus bidirectionally affect baseline and injury-induced nociception. They also find that pain does not affect fear responses, suggesting a hierarchy of survival behaviors that prioritizes predator evasion over attention to noxious stimuli. The study is interesting. However, here are concerns – particularly regarding if the statements made are substantiated by the data- that need to be addressed by the authors before publication.
Major comments:
1. It is unclear that the manipulations are being done on a functionally relevant population. The cFOS in Figure 1 is quite different from the DREADD/mCherry expression for the recordings and manipulations in figure 2/3.
2. The authors claim that inhibiting APC GABA neurons attenuates the effect of predator odor on pain and that activating APC GABA neurons recapitulates the effect of odor on pain. The data in the main and supplementary figures do not necessarily support this claim.
a. The activation of these neurons (hm3d and ChR2 experiments) should recapitulate what happens with the 2MT response. Figure 3 paints a far more complicated picture. Although, the authors state in the abstract “Conversely, activation of APCGABA neurons or the APCGABA-MD circuit recapitulates fear-induced analgesia.” This statement is not supported by figure 3 or 5.
b. APC GABA neuron inhibition affects pain independent of odor. The authors argue that because there was no significant difference between the inhibited groups with and without odor, the effect is not due to a change in baseline sensitivity. At face value this is confusing. First, this was only true for mechanical stimuli which was acknowledged but not discussed. Second, the authors should report the ANOVA interactions in Fig. S7 rather than comparing the two CNO groups. This would show if the effect of inhibition was different with and without 2MT, which I believe is the comparison the authors are trying to make.
c. The fact that only mechanical sensitivity seems to be further heightened by inhibition and the fact that activation produces analgesia even when predator odor is present (and presumably already activating APC neurons) makes it difficult to fully support the claim that this circuit underlies predator odor analgesia and not nociception in general. While it is important and appreciated that the authors showed the effects without odor (inhibition) and with odor (excitation), it would be helpful to explore the possibility that different manipulations might be able to better distinguish baseline nociceptive effects from odor.
i. Could the authors try changing their stimulation and inhibition parameters in a way that would not affect baseline thresholds but would still affect odor-induced analgesia?
d. What proportion of APC GABA neurons are activated by 2MT? Is there subtype specificity that may be confounding the results? Would manipulating 2MT TRAPed APC inhibitory neurons more specifically affect predator odor analgesia and have less of an effect on baseline nociceptive thresholds?
3. It is inappropriate to say that APC GABA neurons ‘encode’ fear-related olfactory information. Based on the data, the strongest conclusion that can be made is that they respond (transiently) to 2MT. Furthermore, the excitatory neurons in the APC also respond, making any conclusions about encoding more difficult.
4. There appears to be a mismatch between the neural activity recordings and the effect of this circuit on pain. How long were mice exposed to odors during the fiber photometry experiments? The neurons show clear bursts in activity, but the increase only lasts a few seconds. How could these neurons influence pain across minutes and hours? It would be beneficial to show neural responses during longer exposures that are similar to those the mice experience during behavioral tests.
a. Relatedly, there is some detail lacking in the results and methods sections on how mice were exposed to the odors during behavioral assays.
5. Figure 5G-I is confusing as presented and the claim based on these data are not currently fully supported. The authors claim that inhibition of APC GABA   MD, “2MT failed to rescue SNI-elicited MD hyperactivity…” (line 299). At minimum, the authors should include mCherry and hM4 groups that were not exposed to 2MT to show the effect in controls and compare it to the effect after inhibition. It would also be helpful to include “SNI” and “2MT” in the labels of these panels and indicate that these data are from MD and not APC slices.
6. While figure 5 (retro-cre) is not miswritten, there remains the caveat that these neurons could have collateral projections.
7. Supplementary figure 9 kind of undercuts the story… a very small proportion of fos expressing neurons seem to project to the MD.
8. As camkII neurons were also activated, it is unclear why they were not functionally tested.
Minor
1. Given the fact that excitatory APC neurons are activated by both aversive and neutral odors it would be interesting to know if APC excitatory neurons also project to MD.
2. What is physiological and pathological pain – these terms are a bit novel for the abstract.
3. Hargreave’s should be written Hargreaves or Hargreaves’
4. The specificity of the transgene targeting using such promoter based viral vectors is always complicated – how often was specificity tested?
In summary, the authors convincingly show that this circuit can modulate pain responses, but more work should be done if the authors wish to make the claim that this pathway is the central mechanism/circuit for innate fear-induced analgesia.

### Reviewer 2

### Reviewer 3

In this study, Jia et al. provide an extensive assessment of the role of the anterior piriform cortex in mediating the analgesic effect of innate fear. The topic is highly interesting but complex as it is not easy to conceptually link the impact of innate fear on pain sensation. To do so the authors exposed mice to the odor of predators and then proceed to a battery of pain-related tests, showing that animals previously exposed to the odor predator exhibit reduced nocifensive behavioral responses.
Using an extensive combination of anatomical, imaging, and functional approaches they progressively identify a GABAergic projections from the anterior proportion of the piriform cortex to the mediodorsal thalamus that may be both necessary and sufficient for this effect. This result calls for partcular attention since long-distance inhibitory projections from cortex to the MD has never been reported before in mice. The amount of experimental work is impressive and all approaches are by themselves state-of-the-art, but the meaning and interpretation of all these experiments also appear as somewhat questionable. In addition, crucial methodological details are missing as explained below.
Methodology/behavioral paradigm
The exact protocol for odor exposure is not clear enough in relation with the many experiments reported. When exactly and for how long are animals exposed to the different odours? Is it acute or multiple exposures? Is it during each beahvioral assay or just before? Dpending on the answers to these questions there may be new issues to consider. Too many crucial details are lacking preventing the reader from understanding what exactly has been done.
For all histological controls, not enough data are provided to document the spread of viral infusion. For all interventions (DREADD and opto), general histology should be provided showing shades of spread for each included individual as is usually the norm.
Without these essential controls/information, the conceptual ground of the whole paper is unclear.
GABAergic projection from cortex to thalamus
The authors should really comment on whether this was expected or not. Very importantly, greater care is needed to ensure that this important claim is unambiguously supported by included data.
For example, neurons that are positive for vgat may also transmit glutamate, how do we know if that is not the case here?
Viral spread into TRN which is mentionned in the paper is guaranteed to yield thalamic inhibition but this is not taken into consideration. The authors also reasonned that there is a higher proportion of GAD2+ proportion of cells labelled for dtomato than it is for CamKII cells (Figure 2c and 2d, the first d should be c though) but the panel c shows very few GAD2+ cells whereas CAMKII+ cells are abundant. This casts further doubt on that inhibitory CT route which would be further fraction at best of those GAD2+ cells (those projecting to the MD). All these issues add on each other, making the whole point not compelling given the importance of the claim.
Taken together, these issues largely undermine the paper to the extent that it is unclear whether the main points could still hold if they can be adequately addressed and making any more minor comments irrelevant at this stage. The paper would also benefit from professional level proof-reading for english.

### Reviewer 4

The manuscript by Jia et al. describes a very interesting set of findings revealing a potential circuit underlying pain suppression by innate fear. Of particular interest this is a novel long-range GABAergic projection originating from Anterior Piriform Cortex (APC) and targeting MD thalamus. While I think the basic story is sound, there are some issues with statistical comparisons and the interpretation of results that need to be addressed. In addition, it is unclear how the slice results relate to the behavioral results – there are questions about how exactly manipulations were done and what were the possible mechanisms that lead to long-lasting effects of 2MT exposure / chemogenetic inhibition persisting into slice experiments.
1. It would be useful to know what % of APC neurons activated by fear are a) GABAergic, b) project to MD, and c) are both.
2. For 4e – what was the protocol for 2MT exposure? Specifically what was the frequency and duration of 2MT exposure, and what was the timing relative to brain slice preparation? What do the authors think is the mechanism underlying this effect?
3. The causal demonstration of the role of this circuit is in Fig. 5 and 6. Fig. 5 shows that chemogenetically inhibiting MD-projecting GABAergic neurons in APC increases pain sensitivity in normal mice and SNI mice exposed to 2MT. Fig. 5g-i show that chemogenetic inhibition of GABAergic APC-MD neurons increases the excitability of MD neurons in 2MT-exposed SNI mice.
a. The protocol for 2MT exposure and chemogenetic inhibition are not explained. Specifically what was the frequency and duration of 2MT exposure? What was the timing of 2MT exposure relative to brain slice preparation? Was chemogenetic inhibition done preceding/during every 2MT exposure, and if not, what was the timing of chemogenetic inhibition relative to 2MT exposure?
b. Does the effect of chemogenetic inhibition on MD neuron excitability depend on 2MT exposure, or does the same effect occur in mice which undergo chemogenetic inhibition but have not been exposed to 2MT? This seems like an important and straightforward experiment.
c. What is the possible mechanism for this? Was there a change in input resistance suggestive of increases in spontaneous inhibitory input (potentially from GABAergic APC-MD terminals) in MD neurons? Did the authors measure spontaneous inhibitory input? This mechanism is important because it’s hard to imagine how transient inhibition of an inhibitory input would end up leading to persistent changes in the excitability of MD neurons.
4. Fig. 6 shows that inhibition of GABAergic APC-MD terminals increases pain sensitivity in mice exposed to 2MT +/- SNI. Based on Supp. Fig 6+7, it seems that the effect is really the same regardless of whether mice have been exposed to 2MT and/or SNI – inhibiting these cells always leads to an exacerbation of pain sensitivity (albeit this effect is smaller in absence of 2MT). So it’s not just that it abolishes the effects of 2MT, but it also seems to increase pain sensitivity at baseline – this is an important point that should be noted explicitly and clearly.
5. Based on Supp Fig. 6c, inhibiting APC-MD GABAergic neurons increases CPA. This means that inhibiting these neurons is aversive, independent of pain. Conversely increases in the activity of these neurons are probably rewarding. This is a caveat that makes the interpretation of Fig. 6i less clear – specifically, the CPP shown in Fig. 6i may not be related to an alleviation of pain but rather to independent rewarding effects of the stimulation.
6. It’s a bit odd to use 20Hz pulse trains to activate eNpHR – its kinetics are too slow to respond to these pulse trains so it’s a bit better / simpler to just use continuous light. Related to this, was the reported light power the peak light power, i.e., each pulse reaches a peak of 5 mW, or was the reported light power of 5 mW the net / average power measured over light ON and light OFF periods?
7. Line 209 – the authors should not report “a trend towards a statistically significant decrease.” The decrease is not statistically significant. They can say that this was a trend that did not reach statistical significance, or they can perform additional experiments to increase the n to confirm that the result does / does not reach statistical significance.
8. Related to this, almost all of the statistical tests are performed as comparisons within a group on two days, where the author report significant changes in the experimental group but not in the control group. Really, this is not appropriate – the authors should perform statistical tests which directly compare the experimental and control groups, either using a 2-way ANOVA, or by calculating a difference score for each animal across the two days and then comparing these difference scores between the experimental and control groups to show a significant difference. I think the authors need to do this, if not in all cases, for their key findings.

### Reviewer 5

In this manuscript by Jia and colleagues, the authors investigate the neural mechanisms by which innate fear suppresses pain sensitivity in male mice, identifying a GABAergic projection from the anterior piriform cortex (APC) to the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) as a key component. Using a combination of viral tracing, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, chemogenetics, and optogenetics, the authors claim to show that innate fear—triggered by predator odor (2MT)—induces analgesia via this corticothalamic circuit.
While the study is methodologically rich and addresses an important topic, several conceptual, methodological, and interpretive issues significantly dampened the excitement about the manuscript and its current impact. The manuscript overstates its mechanistic conclusions. In my opinion, the core effects observed are better interpreted as modulations of pain sensitivity, rather than evidence of a distinct analgesic state induced by innate fear.
Major points:
1. The manuscript relies on the premises that the 2MT odor promotes innate fear, but the behavioral characterization of the 2MT is very poor. The only information we have is supplementary Figure 1, with an example of the trajectories and the overall quantification of freezing.
a. The methods section lacks a description of how freezing is calculated. The authors only mention that it's done via software.
b. Regarding the methods, the authors mention six trials for each odor, but we always see only the averages of the six trials. Is there a desensitization/habituation to the odor? In addition, it's mentioned that there is a one-second exposure of the odor per trial, but there is no mention of how long the wait between trials is.
c. Do all mice display innate fear responses to the odor? Were mice excluded?
d. There is a critical inconsistency in the odor delivery protocols. The method section for the odor exposure to induce innate fear described for the fiber photometry are different from the one described in innate fear detection. More importantly, I could not find any information on how the odor is integrated with the pain assays in the manuscript. Is the odor delivered continuously while the pain assays (like von Frey test, Hargreave's test, etc) are ongoing? Are the mice exposed to it only once before initiating the battery of pain assays or at the beginning of each pain test? The timeline for the behavioural manipulations needs to be clarified.
All these points should be carefully addressed in order to understand the following figures of the manuscript and how exactly innate fear impacts pain sensitivity. This is particularly true since all the key readouts (e.g., increased thresholds, reduced nocifensive responses) may reflect motor suppression (freezing) rather than analgesia.
2. Although not clearly stated, the figures, figure caption and main text suggest that the same mice undergo the series of pain sensitivity tests for each experiment. For example, the same group of mice undergoes all the tests in the main figure 1. This suggests the authors rely on repeated pain testing in the same mice across multiple conditions without proper counterbalancing. This could lead to several problems. Stress-Induced Analgesia (SIA) is a well-documented phenomenon where repeated exposure to stress or pain itself alters subsequent sensitivity, and this could have a significant impact on the overall results and lead to possible confounds. There is no evidence that the pain sensitivity test exposure order was controlled, counterbalanced or test-order randomized. This weakens the overall conclusions of the manuscript.
3. The supplementary figure 6 Shows that modulation (particularly the inactivation) of APC GABA neurons regulates pain sensitivity without innate fear. This undermines the central claim that fear is required for analgesia. In response, the authors add Supplementary Figures 7 and 11, in which a comparison between the pain thresholds following neuronal inhibition with and without innate fear exposure is shown. However, these comparisons are convoluted, spread across multiple figures, and not clearly described. In detail:
a. Supplementary Figure 7 a-b - compared with supplementary figure 6 a-c with main figure 3 a-d
b. Supplementary Figure 7 c-d - compares supplementary figure 10 with main figure 5 a-d
c. Supplementary Figure 7 e-f - compares supplementary figure 11 a-c with main figure 6 a-d
d. And then, Supplementary Figure 11d-g relates to the main figure 6g-l
All of this back and forth is very chaotic and takes the attention away from the fact that there is a modulation of pain sensitivity alone, without the need for innate fear. Moreover, on the main text, the authors claim that these supplementary controls have "no significance differences" (line193-195;) and "did not show any differences in mechanical nociception (line 312-313)" and that is not true, which is simply incorrect based on the actual data of the supplementary figure. Moreover, the results of the thermal pain are not mentioned or compared. The data suggest that APC-GABA neurons modulate pain tonically and do not require fear for their effect. The manuscript selectively emphasizes data that support the fear angle and buries conflicting data in chaotic supplements.
4. No effort is made to dissociate freezing-induced motor suppression from true analgesic effects. Since 2MT induces freezing, reduced reactivity to pain stimuli could reflect behavioral suppression, not analgesia. The rotarod test is used to argue that circuit manipulations do not impair motor function. However, the rotarod primarily assesses gross motor coordination and balance, not fine motor output or spontaneous movement. - Paw withdrawal tests rely on quick reflex-like responses that may not be fully reflected in rotarod performance. Thus, motor slowing, freezing behavior, or motivational changes could still confound nociceptive assays.
5. The authors fail to adequately address the possibility that observed pain suppression results from inhibited motor output (such as freezing) rather than altered pain perception. The rotarod primarily assesses gross motor coordination and balance, not fine motor output or spontaneous movement. - Paw withdrawal tests rely on quick reflex-like responses that may not be fully reflected in rotarod performance. In addition, it seems that the activation of the APC-GABA promotes freezing in naive mice and decreases locomotion. Thus, motor slowing, freezing behavior, or motivational changes could still confound nociceptive assays. There can be a change in pain sensitivity merely because the manipulations impact motion.
6. In several key experiments (e.g., Fig. 2d: 3 mice; Fig. 2g–l: 5 mice per group), sample sizes are extremely small. The authors do not provide power analyses or variance estimates to justify these choices. How did the authors access the statistical power?
Minor points:
1. The introduction lacks referencing, e.g., lines 30, 32, 40, and 46.
2. The data referenced from lines 161 to 168 is not provided. It would be relevant to include such a dataset, yet only mechanical nociception is mentioned; thermal is missing.
3. Fig. 1b—The latency and number of licks or jumps are taken into consideration together, but there is massive variability. These are distinct behaviors and should be analyzed separately.
4. Fig. 1c - How is the % of response for the pinprick test calculated?
5. Fig. 2d - typo, the representative figure is panel c instead of d
6. Fig. 2g-l, heatmaps—not all animals seem to have a modulation of the neuronal activity during the delivery of 2MT. What could be the explanation?
7. Fig. 7 - Why, for physiological pain conditions, was only the thermal pain tested and not the mechanical?
8. Supplementary Figure 3 b-d - anisole group missing, therefore the conclusion on lines 120-121 that "These findings provide additional evidence for the involvement of APC neurons in processing fear-related olfactory information." could potentially be wrong since there is no odor that does not elicit fear responses.
9. Supplementary Figure 3g and j - only cotton swab. Airpuff is missing, and no explanation is provided for it to be the case.
10. Supplementary Figure 4 - The re-exposure to the arena should have been counterbalanced.
11. Supplementary Figure 9 and 11 - Typo, the letters associated with the panels are in CAPS.
The manuscript's conceptual framework offers an important mechanistic insight into how innate fear modulates pain sensitivity via an olfactory-cortical-thalamic GABAergic circuit. It is conceptually valuable and could contribute strongly to understanding how fear can suppress pain and lead to potential therapeutic targets for pain management. However, the current version of this manuscript contains significant interpretive overreach and methodological limitations. The central claim is not supported by the data as presented, and several key results are confounded. With substantial revision and reframing, the core finding—that an APC-GABA-MD circuit modulates pain sensitivity—could still represent a publishable advance, but not in its current conceptual framing as a fear-induced analgesia mechanism.

1. It is unclear that the manipulations are being done on a functionally relevant population. The cFOS in Figure 1 is quite different from the DREADD/mCherry expression for the recordings and manipulations in figure 2/3.
We appreciate the reviewer’s insightful comment regarding the difference between the cFOS patterns and the DREADD/mCherry expression. As shown in original Figure 1d, 2MT exposure activates both inhibitory and excitatory neurons, whereas in Figs. 2 and 3, the DREADD/mCherry experiments specifically target GABAergic neurons, which include a subset of Fos+ neurons. Thus, though partially overlapping, the two groups appeared to unidentical.
To directly address this concern, we now employed the TRAP2 strain, which enables genetic labeling and manipulation of neurons activated by a defined stimulation.1 To this end, we bilaterally injected AAV-VGAT-DIO-hM4Gi-mCherry into the APC of TRAP2 mice, followed by 2MT exposure paired with 4-OHT injection. Using this approach, we were able to specifically manipulate 2MT-activated inhibitory neurons. Inhibiting this ensemble significantly attenuated 2MT-induced fear expression and reduced 2MT-induced analgesia, but did not affect baselines thermal/mechanical nociception or locomotion (Response Fig. 1a-k; revised Fig. 4a-k). These findings establish that 2MT-responsive APCGABA neurons are necessary for innate fear-induced analgesia while being functionally distinct from basal nociceptive processing.
Furthermore, selective activation of 2MT-trapped APC inhibitory neurons was sufficient to evoke freezing and robust analgesia in the absence of 2MT, again without affecting motor performance (Response Fig. 1m-u; revised Fig. 4m-u). These complementary loss- and gain-of-function results demonstrate that 2MT-responsive APCGABA neurons are both necessary and sufficient for innate fear-related analgesia.
We have incorporated these data into the revised manuscript (lines 233-246; 275-282).

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
In this study, Jia et al. provide an extensive assessment of the role of the anterior piriform cortex in mediating the analgesic effect of innate fear. The topic is highly interesting but complex as it is not easy to conceptually link the impact of innate fear on pain sensation. To do so the authors exposed mice to the odor of predators and then proceed to a battery of pain-related tests, showing that animals previously exposed to the odor predator exhibit reduced nocifensive behavioral responses. Using an extensive combination of anatomical, imaging, and functional approaches they progressively identify a GABAergic projections from the anterior proportion of the piriform cortex to the mediodorsal thalamus that may be both necessary and sufficient for this effect. This result calls for particular attention since long-distance inhibitory projections from cortex to the MD has never been reported before in mice. The amount of experimental work is impressive and all approaches are by themselves state-of-the-art, but the meaning and interpretation of all these experiments also appear as somewhat questionable. In addition, crucial methodological details are missing as explained below.
RESPONSE: We sincerely appreciate the reviewer's thoughtful evaluation of our study and the important concerns. Below we provide point-by-point responses to strengthen the manuscript.
Methodology/behavioral paradigm
The exact protocol for odor exposure is not clear enough in relation with the many experiments reported. When exactly and for how long are animals exposed to the different odours? Is it acute or multiple exposures? Is it during each beahvioral assay or just before? Dpending on the answers to these questions there may be new issues to consider. Too many crucial details are lacking preventing the reader from understanding what exactly has been done.
We thank the reviewer for raising this important point regarding the odor exposure protocol. We have now revised the Methods section to include detailed, step-by-step description of each procedure to ensure full experimental transparency:
• Pain behavior assays: Mice were first acclimated to the behavioral chamber for 30 minutes prior to testing. After acclimation, a continuous 2MT (or control solvent) odor was introduced by placing a filter paper saturated with the stimulus at the top of the chamber. Measurements of thermal or mechanical sensitivity (Hargreaves and von Frey tests) began 2 minutes after odor onset, and the odor stimulus was maintained throughout the entire testing session. This ensured that the animals remained in a sustained state of innate fear during nociceptive assessment.
• Odor-evoked calcium imaging: Mice were habituated for 30 minutes in a square testing box before odor presentation. Odor stimuli (water, anisole, or 2MT) were delivered either by air puff or cotton swab, with six repeated trials per odor and 1-minute inter-trial intervals. Each odor exposure lasted 1 second per trial. For delivery, a Pasteur pipette or cotton swab containing 50 μl of odor solution was briefly introduced into the chamber.
• Electrophysiology experiments: Mice received intraperitoneal CNO (30 minutes prior) to either 1-hour 2MT or water exposure, after which acute brain slices containing the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus were prepared for electrophysiological recordings.
We apologize for the lack of methodological details in the original submission. The revised manuscript now adds these procedures. The revised manuscript now includes these clarifications in the Methods section to facilitate reproducibility and interpretation of our findings.

To fully address the reviewer’s recommendation, we conducted a new, independently replicated chemogenetic experiment using TRAP2 mice, for which viral expression was systematically analyzed and documented for every individual animal. The revised supplementary Fig. 4 (Response Figure 11) now provides representative micrographs and schematic reconstructions for all subjects, aligned to standard brain atlas plates to clearly illustrate the extent and reproducibility of viral spread.

GABAergic projection from cortex to thalamus
The authors should really comment on whether this was expected or not. Very importantly, greater care is needed to ensure that this important claim is unambiguously supported by included data.
We thank the reviewer for this important point. The identification of a long-range GABAergic projection from the anterior piriform cortex (APC) to the mediodorsal (MD) thalamus was indeed unexpected, as the cortico-thalamic pathway is classically considered glutamatergic4,5. Based on the established findings regarding long-range cortical GABAergic projections (auditory cortex→lateral amygdala pathway6, and medial prefrontal cortex→to the retrosplenial cortex pathway7), our study provides evidence for the existence and functional significance of a GABAergic projection from the APC to the MD.
Specifically, our multidisciplinary approach combining viral tracing, optogenetics, chemogenetics and electrophysiological recordings provide the anatomical evidence of APC→MD inhibitory projection, and demonstrates crucial role of the APC→MD pathway in innate fear-induced analgesia.
The discovery of this APC→MD pathway aligns with the growing recognition of cortical long-range inhibitory circuits as important regulators of distant brain regions (such as amygdala and cortex)6,7. Our results extend this emerging paradigm to the olfactory system, revealing a previously uncharacterized inhibitory corticothalamic circuit that may coordinate cross-regional behavioral outputs during threat perception.
These points have been incorporated into the revised discussion (lines 486-487; 489-494).
For example, neurons that are positive for vgat may also transmit glutamate, how do we know if that is not the case here?
We thank the reviewer for highlighting this important point. Indeed, a subset of VGAT-positive neurons has been reported to co-release glutamate under certain conditions. While the precise incidence of such co-transmission within the specific cortical population we targeted remains to be determined, evidence from the mouse cerebral cortex indicates that co-expression of VGAT and VGLUT1 at the synaptic level is rare, approximately 3.6 ± 0.2% of VGAT⁺ puncta8. Importantly, the net physiological effect of optogenetic activation in our study was pain suppression, a response that is inconsistent with predominant glutamatergic excitation. Thus, while we cannot completely exclude the possibility that a small subset of VGAT⁺ neurons may co-release glutamate, our functional and anatomical data strongly support that the observed effect is primarily mediated through GABAergic transmission. Future intersectional strategies selectively deleting glutamatergic signaling components in this population will help clarify any potential modulatory contribution of co-released glutamate to the observed fear-induced analgesia.

As now documented in the Response Fig. 12, we confirmed that in the TRAP2 mice included in the final behavioral analyses, viral expression was largely restricted to the intended cortical target regions, with no detectable spread into the TRN.

Methodologically, the limited overlap may partly stem from inherent constraints of retrograde tracing, as some activated MD-projecting neurons might not be labeled. Biologically, however, the high activation rate within this subpopulation suggests functional specificity rather than weak circuit engagement. These findings indicate that, although numerically limited, a specialized subset of MD-projecting APCGABA neurons is preferentially recruited by 2MT and exerts a functionally significant influence on fear-related analgesia. In addition, given that only ~40 % of APC GABA neurons were activated by 2MT (revised supplementary Fig. 12a-c), we recognized that broad manipulation of APCGABA neurons could confound odor-specific effects. Reviewer #5 (Remarks to the Author):
In this manuscript by Jia and colleagues, the authors investigate the neural mechanisms by which innate fear suppresses pain sensitivity in male mice, identifying a GABAergic projection from the anterior piriform cortex (APC) to the mediodorsal thalamus (MD) as a key component. Using a combination of viral tracing, electrophysiology, fiber photometry, chemogenetics, and optogenetics, the authors claim to show that innate fear—triggered by predator odor (2MT)—induces analgesia via this corticothalamic circuit.
While the study is methodologically rich and addresses an important topic, several conceptual, methodological, and interpretive issues significantly dampened the excitement about the manuscript and its current impact. The manuscript overstates its mechanistic conclusions. In my opinion, the core effects observed are better interpreted as modulations of pain sensitivity, rather than evidence of a distinct analgesic state induced by innate fear.
Major points:
1. The manuscript relies on the premises that the 2MT odor promotes innate fear, but the behavioral characterization of the 2MT is very poor. The only information we have is supplementary Figure 1, with an example of the trajectories and the overall quantification of freezing.
We thank the reviewer for this important critique regarding the behavioral characterization of 2MT-induced fear responses and agree that detailed behavioral validation is essential. 2MT is a well-established innate fear odor. This phenomenon has been extensively documented and replicated in multiple independent reports. In the revised manuscript, we now explicitly cite these foundational studies and clarify that our behavioral results (Supplementary Fig. 1) are consistent with this well-established literature11,12.
a. The methods section lacks a description of how freezing is calculated. The authors only mention that it's done via software.
We thank the reviewer for pointing out the need for additional detail regarding the freezing quantification. We have now included the following description in the Methods section:
“The experiment was conducted using the SuperFcs Conditional Fear Conditioning System, which was provided by Shanghai XinRuan Information Technology Co., Ltd. For data analysis, we utilized the built-in SuperMaze animal behavior video analysis software, Version 2.0. This software allowed us to adjust the Mobility/Immobility threshold to accurately differentiate between the mobility and immobility states of the mice, as well as modify the Immobility/Freezing threshold to effectively distinguish between immobility and freezing states induced by fear.
After conducting multiple tests, we determined the optimal initial values displayed on the software to be a Mobility/Immobility threshold of 16 and an Immobility/Freezing threshold of 19. Subsequently, we proceeded with the formal experiment. These preset parameters were applied consistently across all freezing-related experiments in this study.”
b. Regarding the methods, the authors mention six trials for each odor, but we always see only the averages of the six trials. Is there a desensitization/habituation to the odor? In addition, it's mentioned that there is a one-second exposure of the odor per trial, but there is no mention of how long the wait between trials is.
We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful question regarding potential odor habituation. To address this, we analyzed trial-by-trial photometry data within each session in both transgenic and C57 mice. The analysis revealed stable calcium response magnitudes across all six trials of anisole or 2MT exposure (Response Fig. 18; revised Supplemental Fig. 5), indicating negligible habituation under our experimental conditions. We have incorporated these data into the revised manuscript (lines 161-165).
To minimize potential olfactory adaptation, a 1-min inter-trial interval was maintained between successive odor trials in our experiments. This interval was chosen based on prior literature showing that it provides sufficient recovery time for olfactory receptor cell to reset after stimulation13. We have added the detailed exposure protocol in the Methods part (lines 612-619).

d. There is a critical inconsistency in the odor delivery protocols. The method section for the odor exposure to induce innate fear described for the fiber photometry are different from the one described in innate fear detection.
